articles.title: I Captured 89 Product Pages in Less Than 30 Seconds. Then Codex Built the Presentation.
articles.description: How I used Playwright to capture product pages and gave Codex the screenshots and GitHub backlog to build an editable PowerPoint deck.
articles.body_html:
In the first article in this series, I described how I take a product from a brainstorm to a production release with AI. In the follow-up about finding the first users, I wrote about the difficulty of reaching beyond my LinkedIn circles.

Explaining the product is part of that work. Someone encountering it for the first time needs to see what they could do with it. This article looks at how I collected the product visuals and reused them in a presentation.

I needed current screenshots of a product I am building. Not three polished pages for a landing page, but every routable page in the application, including the ones that were not linked from the navigation.

Doing that manually would have been a small project of its own: find the routes, open each page, wait for it to render, take a full-page screenshot, name the file, and keep track of what I had missed.

Instead, I gave the job to GPT-6 Luna with Playwright.

The result from my run was 89 screenshots in less than 30 seconds, using 1.76 credits.

That is close enough to free for a task that would normally consume hours of repetitive attention. More importantly, those screenshots did not remain a folder of images. I later gave them to Codex together with the GitHub issues and epics for the product, then used its PowerPoint integration to create an editable presentation.

The useful lesson was not simply that a small model was cheap. It was that the inexpensive step created evidence for the more demanding step that followed.

The screenshot task was repetitive, but not trivial

"Take screenshots of my application" would have been an easy prompt to write and a bad one to trust.

An agent could visit the home page and the pages exposed in the main menu, save a few files, and report success. That might look convincing while missing secondary routes, pages still under development, or screens reachable only through a direct URL.

I needed a result I could inspect, count, and reuse. This was the prompt:

Use Playwright to visit every routable page in the app, including pages not linked in the navigation. Take a full-page screenshot of each page and save the PNGs under docs/screenshots/. Name each file with a two-digit number followed by a descriptive route name, ordered by the app's navigation menu; place pages that aren't in the menu afterward. Use a consistent desktop viewport, wait for each page to finish rendering before capturing it, and verify that every route was visited and every screenshot was saved. Don't include reusable components or partials as separate pages.

The wording matters because each clause closes a predictable gap.

"Every routable page" forces the agent to inspect the application rather than behave like a visitor clicking through the menu. Calling out pages that are not in the navigation makes that expectation explicit. Full-page capture prevents a collection of arbitrary viewport crops, while the naming convention makes 89 files reviewable without manually sorting them afterward.

The last sentence establishes the boundary. I wanted user-facing pages, not every component or partial that happened to exist in the codebase.

It is a prompt, but it behaves more like a small specification. The output location, order, file format, viewport behavior, completion condition, and exclusions are all visible. That makes the task suitable for a low-cost model because success does not depend on whether I like the prose of its final answer. I can check the files.

Why I used GPT-6 Luna

I do not need the most capable model for every task.

This job required tool use, persistence, and basic interpretation of the application's route structure. It did not require a product strategy, a nuanced argument, or a presentation narrative. Once the route boundary was clear, the rest was a mechanical browser operation.

That made GPT-6 Luna a reasonable choice. In this particular run, it completed the capture with 1.76 credits. I am deliberately describing that as a measured result, not a permanent price promise: credit systems and model behavior can change.

The economic point still holds. Model selection should follow the work. If a cheaper model can complete a bounded task and the result can be verified independently, paying for more reasoning does not automatically produce more value.

The important word is verified.

For a screenshot job, I want to check at least four things:

  • The route list matches the application.
  • The expected number of PNG files exists.
  • The images use the intended viewport and have plausible dimensions.
  • None of the pages was captured in a loading, error, empty, or signed-out state.

A folder containing 89 files proves that 89 files were created. It does not prove that every page is correct. Authentication, role-specific routes, feature flags, dynamic parameters, and slow data loading can all make a screenshot set look complete when it is not.

The screenshots became a product artifact

The surprise was not the speed. It was how useful the folder became afterward.

Product screenshots are often treated as disposable material for documentation or marketing. This set was closer to a visual inventory. It showed the product as it existed across 89 routes at one moment, including screens I would not have selected for a polished demo.

That distinction matters when a product is still under development. The navigation shows what users can reach easily. The route inventory shows what the application contains. The GitHub roadmap shows what I intend to build. Those are three different views, and they do not always agree.

The screenshots gave me the current implementation. My GitHub issues and epics contained the intent behind it: planned capabilities, larger product themes, and work that might not yet be visible in the interface.

Together, they formed better input for a presentation than a prompt such as "create a deck about my product."

Why I switched to Codex for the presentation

The next task was no longer mechanical.

A useful product presentation needs selection. It has to decide which screens explain the product, how they support the story, where the current implementation ends, and where the roadmap begins. It also needs visual hierarchy, consistent layouts, and an editable output that I can continue working with.

The audience changes that selection. For the walkthrough I discussed in the previous article, I would choose the screens that explain one task a prospective user cares about. A stakeholder presentation may also need the roadmap and the reasoning behind planned work. The same screenshot inventory can support both, with a different story and a different scope.

This is where I preferred Codex. Its integration with PowerPoint is particularly useful because the result is a real presentation rather than a textual outline pretending to be one. Codex could work from the screenshots, inspect the GitHub issues and epics, structure the product story, and place the visual evidence into an editable deck.

The two sources played different roles:

  • The screenshots showed what existed.
  • GitHub showed the tracked product direction.

That reduced a common failure in generated decks: confidently describing a product that exists only in the prompt. The presentation could be grounded in the interface while still explaining what I was developing next.

It still required review. Issues can be outdated, a screenshot can show an unfinished state, and a model can create a clean narrative by hiding contradictions that the product team actually needs to discuss. I checked the deck against both sources rather than treating the generated slides as the source of truth.

Cheap execution and expensive judgment

I see these as two different classes of work.

The screenshot task was bounded and countable. There was a route list, a folder, a naming rule, and a file count. GPT-6 Luna did not need to understand why page 47 mattered to the product strategy. It needed to open the page correctly and save the image in the right place.

The presentation task required judgment. Which screenshots belong together? Which GitHub issues explain a visible workflow? What should a viewer understand after ten minutes? Which roadmap items are plans rather than shipped features? Those questions benefit from stronger reasoning and a tool that can implement the answer directly in PowerPoint.

Using one model for both jobs would have been simpler to describe, but not necessarily better. The handoff between them was the useful design:

  1. Use Playwright to turn the running product into a verified screenshot set.
  2. Preserve that set under docs/screenshots/ as a reusable project artifact.
  3. Combine the visual inventory with GitHub issues and epics.
  4. Use Codex and the PowerPoint integration for synthesis and implementation.
  5. Review the deck against the application and the issue tracker.

The low-cost step did not compete with the higher-value step. It improved its input.

What I would tighten before running it again

The original prompt worked well, but there are a few controls I would add for a production workflow.

First, I would ask for a route manifest next to the PNG files, recording the route, filename, page title, HTTP status, and capture result. That would make the coverage easier to audit than relying on filenames alone.

Second, I would define how authenticated and parameterized routes should be handled. A route such as /projects/:id is not one page in practice, and different roles may see different interfaces at the same URL.

Third, I would add an explicit privacy check. Screenshots can capture test customers, email addresses, tokens, internal URLs, or other information that should never enter a public article or presentation.

Finally, I would separate capture from approval. The agent can create the inventory, but a human should decide which screens are safe, current, and useful enough to leave the repository.

The practical takeaway

The 1.76-credit result is a good hook, but it is not the main reason I will reuse this workflow.

The real value came from choosing tools according to the shape of the work. GPT-6 Luna handled a repetitive browser task with a clear definition of done. Codex handled the part that required product context, narrative choices, GitHub evidence, and a polished PowerPoint artifact.

If you are building a product, do not start the presentation with a blank slide and a vague prompt. Start by capturing what the product actually is. Then connect that evidence to the work you have planned.

The cheapest useful model can create the evidence that makes the more capable model worth using.

AI assisted with editing and creating the diagrams for this article.

articles.title: How to Make Idempotent Replays Skip Rate Limiting in NestJS
articles.description: Imagine you're using @nestjs/throttler and @nestjs/idempotency together.  Everything works fine until...
articles.body_html:
Imagine you're using @nestjs/throttler and @nestjs/idempotency together.

Everything works fine until you notice something: replaying an idempotent request still consumes your rate-limit quota.

That's a problem.

A client sends a request with an Idempotency-Key. The server processes it successfully and stores the result. Later, the client retries the same request because it didn't receive the original response.

The whole point of idempotency is to return the previous result without executing the handler again. So why should a replay consume another rate-limit slot?

Let's look at why this happens and how to fix it without implementing your own rate-limiting algorithm.

Why does this happen?

The important thing to understand is NestJS request lifecycle.

Guards run before interceptors.

A simplified request flow looks like this:

Incoming Request
      |
      v
   Guards
      |
      v
 Global Interceptors
      |
      v
 Route Interceptors
      |
      v
  Controller
      |
      v
   Handler

Now consider our setup:

  • ThrottlerGuard is registered globally using APP_GUARD.
  • IdempotencyInterceptor is registered globally by @nestjs/idempotency.

When a replay arrives, the global rate limiter runs first. At this point, the idempotency interceptor hasn't had a chance to inspect the request.

The request consumes quota, and only afterward does the idempotency interceptor recognize the replay and return the stored response.

We need to change that execution order logically, without breaking the global rate-limiting setup.

The idea: Defer rate-limit enforcement

Instead of enforcing rate limits globally for every request, we'll introduce a way to defer enforcement for specific routes.

The idea is simple:

  1. Mark a route that needs deferred rate limiting.
  2. Make the global rate-limit guard skip that route.
  3. Move the actual rate-limit enforcement into a route-level interceptor.
  4. Let the idempotency interceptor decide whether the request should continue.

The key is that a replay never reaches the route-level interceptor.

Let's implement it.

1. Create a decorator to mark deferred routes

First, we need a custom decorator that adds metadata to a route.

// deferred-rate-limit.decorator.ts

import { SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';

export const DEFERRED_RATE_LIMIT_KEY = 'app:deferred-rate-limit';

export function DeferredRateLimit(): MethodDecorator {
  return SetMetadata(DEFERRED_RATE_LIMIT_KEY, true);
}

This decorator doesn't perform any rate limiting. It simply tells our global guard that enforcement for this route should happen later.

2. Update the global rate-limit guard

Now we extend our existing throttler guard.

Instead of completely replacing ThrottlerGuard, we keep the original implementation and add one small condition.

// deferred-rate-limit.guard.ts

export class DeferredRateLimitGuard extends RedisThrottlerGuard {
  override async canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const deferred = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<boolean>(
      DEFERRED_RATE_LIMIT_KEY,
      [context.getHandler(), context.getClass()],
    );

    if (deferred) {
      return true;
    }

    return super.canActivate(context);
  }
}

That's it.

For normal routes, everything works exactly as before.

For routes marked with @DeferredRateLimit(), the global guard returns true without calling the throttler.

Important: We're not disabling rate limiting. We're only moving its enforcement to another point in the request lifecycle.

3. Enforce the rate limit inside an interceptor

Next, we create an interceptor responsible for enforcing the deferred rate limit.

// deferred-rate-limit.interceptor.ts

@Injectable()
export class DeferredRateLimitInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(
    private readonly throttlerGuard: RedisThrottlerGuard,
  ) {}

  intercept(
    context: ExecutionContext,
    next: CallHandler,
  ): Promise<Observable<unknown>> {
    return this.throttlerGuard
      .canActivate(context)
      .then(() => next.handle());
  }
}

Notice something important here.

We're not implementing another rate-limiting algorithm.

We're reusing the existing RedisThrottlerGuard and calling its canActivate() method directly.

This means we still use the same:

  • Redis storage.
  • Throttling policies.
  • Key generation.
  • @Throttle() metadata.
  • Rate-limit headers and throttling exceptions.

We're only changing when the existing rate limiter runs.

4. Make the guard injectable

Since the interceptor needs an instance of RedisThrottlerGuard, we expose it through a shared module.

// throttler-enforcement.module.ts

@Module({
  imports: [throttlerModule],
  providers: [RedisThrottlerGuard],
  exports: [RedisThrottlerGuard],
})
export class ThrottlerEnforcementModule {}

The feature module imports this module, so the interceptor can use the existing throttler configuration and storage.

Keep this infrastructure inside your shared throttling layer instead of duplicating it in feature modules.

5. Apply everything to an endpoint

Now we can combine the decorators.

@Post('challenge')
@DeferredRateLimit()
@Throttle({ short: { limit: 2, ttl: seconds(120) } })
@UseInterceptors(DeferredRateLimitInterceptor)
@Idempotent(challengeIdempotentOptions)
requestChallenge(@Body() body: ChallengeRequestBody) {
  return this.enrollmentsService.requestChallenge(body.phoneNumber);
}

The order of the interceptors is what makes this work.

With the global idempotency interceptor wrapping the route-level interceptor, the request flow becomes:

Incoming Request
      |
      v
Global Guards
      |
      | Deferred route? Skip throttling.
      |
      v
Global IdempotencyInterceptor
      |
      | Acquire idempotency key
      |
      +---- Completed replay?
      |          |
      |          v
      |     Return stored response
      |     (No rate-limit check)
      |
      +---- Key already in use?
      |          |
      |          v
      |     Return 409 Conflict
      |     (No rate-limit check)
      |
      v
Route-level Interceptor
      |
      v
Rate-limit enforcement
      |
      v
Controller Handler

For a new request, the idempotency interceptor acquires the key and continues down the interceptor chain. That's when our route-level interceptor enforces the rate limit.

For a completed replay, the idempotency interceptor returns the stored response without calling the next interceptor.

The same applies to an in-flight duplicate: the idempotency package rejects it before the deferred rate limiter gets executed.

That's exactly what we want.

6. Don't forget to test the actual quota

One important detail: don't verify this behavior only by checking that the handler wasn't executed.

The handler might be skipped while the rate limiter still consumes quota.

A better approach is to inspect the actual rate-limit counters in Redis.

For example:

const before = await hitCount(tracker, 'short');

const replay = await postChallenge(app, {
  key: existingKey,
  tracker,
});

const after = await hitCount(tracker, 'short');

expect(replay.status).toBe(202);
expect(replay.headers['idempotent-replayed']).toBe('true');
expect(after).toBe(before);

Also test an in-flight duplicate and, even more importantly, a replay when the client's rate-limit quota is already exhausted.

That last scenario proves the behavior we're trying to achieve: an existing idempotent operation can be replayed even when a new request from the same client would receive 429 Too Many Requests.

A few things worth remembering

There are a couple of details you shouldn't overlook:

Don't skip rate limiting just because a request contains an Idempotency-Key header. A new request can have a perfectly valid idempotency key too. The idempotency layer must decide whether the request is a replay or a new operation.

Keep the original @Throttle() metadata. There's no reason to duplicate limits or maintain a separate rate-limiting implementation.

Be careful with interceptor registration order. The global idempotency interceptor must wrap the route-level deferred interceptor. Otherwise, the rate limiter might run before the idempotency decision.

A deferred route must always have a downstream enforcement mechanism. If you add @DeferredRateLimit() but forget @UseInterceptors(DeferredRateLimitInterceptor), that route won't be rate-limited.

The interesting part of this solution isn't writing another rate limiter. It's understanding how NestJS Guards and Interceptors interact.

By skipping the global guard for selected routes and reusing the existing throttler inside a route-level interceptor, we can make idempotent replays bypass rate-limit enforcement without sacrificing the original throttling policies.

A small change in execution order, but an important improvement when building reliable APIs with NestJS.

articles.title: Set Up a WordPress Staging-to-Production Workflow with Git
articles.description: We've all done it. You change one line of CSS directly on the live site, hit save, and the homepage...
articles.body_html:
We've all done it. You change one line of CSS directly on the live site, hit save, and the homepage turns into modern art.

The fix is boring and it works: write and test your changes on a staging copy of the site, keep your code in Git, and push to production only when everything looks right. This guide sets that up in about 30 minutes. No paid plugins, no deployment platform to learn.

The idea in one minute

Two sites, two branches, one rule.

Site URL Git branch
Staging staging.example.com staging
Production example.com main

The rule: code moves up (local → staging → production). Content moves down (production → staging).

Git tracks your theme (or custom plugin). It does not track your database, your uploads, or wp-config.php. Posts, pages, and settings live in the database, so they never travel through Git. If you remember only one thing from this article, remember that.

What you need

  • A WordPress site on a host that gives you SSH access. Check this before you start, because without SSH this workflow doesn't work.
  • A GitHub account.
  • A recent version of Git on your computer (2.28 or newer, for the git init -b flag below).
  • A subdomain for staging.

I used Hostinger for this setup. If you want to do the same, this link gets you 20% off. It's a referral link, so I may earn a commission if you buy through it. On Hostinger, SSH is available on Premium plans and above, but not on Single plans, so pick accordingly. Everything below works on any host that gives you SSH and Git.

Step 1: Put your theme in a Git repo

We'll version just the theme, since that's where most custom code lives. The same pattern works for a custom plugin.

Name the GitHub repository exactly like your theme folder (here, my-theme). It makes the server steps simpler later.

cd wp-content/themes/my-theme
git init -b main
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"

Create an empty repository on GitHub (no README, no .gitignore), then connect it and create the staging branch:

git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/my-theme.git
git push -u origin main
git checkout -b staging
git push -u origin staging

If your theme has a build step, add node_modules/ to a .gitignore file before your first commit. Nobody wants 40,000 files of node_modules in a repo.

Step 2: Create the staging site

  1. Create the subdomain staging.example.com in your hosting panel.
  2. Install a fresh WordPress there, using the same database table prefix as production. You'll find production's prefix in its wp-config.php (the $table_prefix line, usually wp_). If the prefixes differ, the imported database won't be recognized.
  3. Set up SSL for the subdomain.

Now copy production's plugins and uploads over. The database will say which plugins are active, so they need to exist on staging too. Set two variables first (use your real folders; in hPanel, the Subdomains page shows the folder for your subdomain):

PROD=~/domains/example.com/public_html
STAGING=~/domains/example.com/public_html/staging

mkdir -p $STAGING/wp-content/plugins $STAGING/wp-content/uploads
cp -r $PROD/wp-content/plugins/. $STAGING/wp-content/plugins/
cp -r $PROD/wp-content/uploads/. $STAGING/wp-content/uploads/

If you use a parent theme, copy it from wp-content/themes the same way. Your own theme comes from Git in the next step.

Next, copy the database. If WP-CLI is available on your server (check with wp --info), it takes a few commands. Export from the production folder:

cd $PROD
wp db export ~/prod.sql

Then import into staging and fix the URLs:

cd $STAGING
wp db import ~/prod.sql
wp search-replace 'https://example.com' 'https://staging.example.com' --all-tables --skip-columns=guid
wp option update blog_public 0

The last command tells search engines to ignore the staging site. Nobody needs a duplicate of your site showing up on Google.

After the import, staging uses production's user accounts, so log in with your production username and password.

No WP-CLI? A migration plugin like All-in-One WP Migration can do the same copy.

Step 3: Let your servers pull from GitHub

Each server needs permission to read your private repo. You'll use a deploy key, which is a key pair that can only read one repository.

SSH into your server and generate it:

mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "wp-deploy" -f ~/.ssh/github_deploy -N ""
cat ~/.ssh/github_deploy.pub

Copy the output. In your GitHub repo, go to Settings → Deploy keys → Add deploy key, paste it, and leave "Allow write access" unchecked.

Tell SSH to use that key for GitHub:

cat >> ~/.ssh/config << 'EOF'
Host github.com
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/github_deploy
  IdentitiesOnly yes
EOF
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config

Test it:

ssh -T git@github.com

The first time, SSH asks whether to trust GitHub's host key. Type yes. Then you should see a message saying you've successfully authenticated. GitHub doesn't give shell access, so the message ends with a note about that. That's normal.

If staging and production live in the same hosting account, one key covers both. Now clone the theme on each site. The commands below use the $PROD and $STAGING variables from Step 2. If you opened a new SSH session since then, set them again first.

Staging (a fresh WordPress doesn't have your theme yet, so this is a plain clone):

cd $STAGING/wp-content/themes
git clone -b staging git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/my-theme.git

Production (the live theme folder already exists, so clone next to it, then swap and keep a backup outside the themes folder):

cd $PROD/wp-content/themes
git clone -b main git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/my-theme.git my-theme-new
mv my-theme ~/my-theme-backup
mv my-theme-new my-theme

If the clone fails, nothing has changed on your live site. If it works, the swap takes a second. Keep the backup for a while. Future you will say thanks.

Open both sites in a browser and make sure they still look right before you continue.

Step 4: Deploy automatically with GitHub Actions

You could SSH in and run git pull by hand every time. You'd forget within a week. Let GitHub do it.

You need a second key pair, this time so GitHub Actions can log in to your server. Create it on your computer:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "github-actions" -f ./actions_key -N ""
  • Add the contents of actions_key.pub to your server's authorized keys. On Hostinger, that's hPanel → SSH Access → add an SSH key. Elsewhere, append it to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
  • Keep actions_key (the private one) for the next step, then delete both files from your computer.

In your GitHub repo, go to Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions and add these repository secrets:

Secret Value
SSH_HOST Your server's IP or hostname
SSH_PORT Your SSH port (on Hostinger shared hosting it's 65002, and hPanel shows it)
SSH_USER Your SSH username
SSH_KEY The full contents of actions_key

Then add this file to your repo at .github/workflows/deploy.yml. Edit the two THEME_PATH lines to match your server:

name: Deploy theme

on:
  push:
    branches: [staging, main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Pull latest code on the server
        env:
          SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.SSH_KEY }}
          SSH_HOST: ${{ secrets.SSH_HOST }}
          SSH_PORT: ${{ secrets.SSH_PORT }}
          SSH_USER: ${{ secrets.SSH_USER }}
          BRANCH: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          if [ "$BRANCH" = "main" ]; then
            THEME_PATH="~/domains/example.com/public_html/wp-content/themes/my-theme"
          else
            THEME_PATH="~/domains/example.com/public_html/staging/wp-content/themes/my-theme"
          fi

          mkdir -p ~/.ssh
          echo "$SSH_KEY" > ~/.ssh/deploy_key
          chmod 600 ~/.ssh/deploy_key
          ssh-keyscan -p "$SSH_PORT" "$SSH_HOST" >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
          ssh -i ~/.ssh/deploy_key -p "$SSH_PORT" "$SSH_USER@$SSH_HOST" \
            "cd $THEME_PATH && git pull --ff-only origin $BRANCH"

Commit this file on staging and push. Then merge it into main and push again. From now on, pushing to staging updates the staging site, and pushing to main updates production. You can watch each run in the Actions tab of your repo.

If your staging and production sites are on different hosting accounts, you'll need separate host, user, and key values for each. Add them as extra secrets and pick them in the if block the same way.

Your daily workflow 

# 1. Start a branch for your change
git checkout staging
git pull
git checkout -b fix/header-spacing

# 2. Work, test locally, commit
git add .
git commit -m "Fix header spacing on mobile"

# 3. Merge into staging and push (auto-deploys to staging)
git checkout staging
git merge fix/header-spacing
git push

# 4. Check staging.example.com in a browser. Click around. Be suspicious.

# 5. Happy? Merge into main and push (auto-deploys to production)
git checkout main
git pull
git merge staging
git push

Step 4 is the whole point of this setup, so don't skip it.

Rolling back

If something slips through, undo it with Git instead of panicking in a file manager. Find the bad commit and revert it:

git checkout main
git log --oneline
git revert COMMIT-HASH
git push

That creates a new commit that undoes the bad one, and the deploy runs again. Your history stays intact. If the bad commit is a merge commit, use git revert -m 1 COMMIT-HASH instead.

Then bring the fix back to staging so the two branches agree:

git checkout staging
git merge main
git push

Things that will bite you

  • Don't edit theme files on the server. The next git pull can fail because the server copy has changes Git doesn't know about. Make all edits locally.
  • Database changes don't deploy. New pages, widget settings, and page-builder layouts live in the database. Build them on staging if you want, but you'll have to redo them on production, or sync the database deliberately.
  • Refresh staging from production now and then. Repeat the database part of Step 2 so staging doesn't drift away from the real site. This overwrites the staging database, so don't do it in the middle of testing something.
  • Keep emails in check on staging. A staging copy with real customer data can send real emails. Install an SMTP-blocking plugin there, or disable outgoing mail.

Wrapping up

Once this is running, deploying becomes a git push and a short wait. Your live site stays calm, and the homepage stays a homepage.

Need a host for this setup? Get 20% off Hostinger with my referral link.

articles.title: The one-line fix that would have hidden 110 GB of videos again
articles.description: TL;DR: A folder move made 207 videos (about 110 GB) disappear from a media library, even though...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: A folder move made 207 videos (about 110 GB) disappear from a media library, even though every file was safe. A longer timeout would have hidden the bug, not fixed it. The real fix was choosing one source of truth and designing for the moment a move is only half done.

What happened

I work on a client platform with a media library: photos, videos and documents in nested folders. The files live in an S3-compatible bucket, and a Postgres database (behind Hasura) describes every folder and file.

A user moved and renamed two folders full of videos. Both requests timed out. The folders now showed up in their new place, but empty.

Nothing had been deleted. Every video was still in storage. Nobody could see them.

Why the videos disappeared

A folder's path existed in two places:

Database:  folder row → path = "Projects/Launch/"
Storage:   objects    → "Projects/Launch/intro.mp4", ...

The old move code did three things in one request:

  1. Update the folder row to its new path.
  2. Copy every file to the new path in storage, then delete the original.
  3. Update each file row.

Step 1 finished. Step 2 started copying the first video and hit the function's 6-second timeout. The request died with the folder row pointing at the new path and every file still sitting under the old one.

That alone was recoverable. What made the files vanish was the listing code. It asked storage for objects under the folder's new path and dropped any file it couldn't find there. The database said the folder had moved, storage said the files hadn't, and the listing trusted storage. So the folder looked empty.

We repaired it by hand. Later that day, one folder broke again the same way.

The one-line fix

Raise the timeout. It's the first thing anyone would suggest, human or AI, and for a small folder it would even work.

It doesn't hold up:

  • A single 3.9 GB copy takes about 65 seconds. A folder of videos can take far longer than a request is allowed to run, and API gateways cap requests at around 29 seconds by default.
  • Even when a slow move finishes, it spends minutes half done, with some files copied and some not. Files are hidden for that whole window.
  • If it fails partway, we're back where we started.

A longer timeout makes the bug rarer and harder to reproduce. It doesn't remove it.

Where should the truth live?

The bug came from two systems holding the same fact, where is this file?, with nothing to keep them in agreement during a move.

So we picked one:

The database decides where a file belongs. Storage only records where its bytes are right now.

A file belongs to its parent folder, and a folder row always holds its current path. A file's storage key can lag behind for a while, and that's fine.

The design

1. The move becomes instant and database-only. The request validates, queues a background job, updates the folder paths (and any share links to them) in the database, and returns. It never touches the files themselves. The user sees the folder in its new place straight away, with every file listed.

2. A background worker moves the bytes. The job goes onto a queue (AWS SQS), and a separate worker picks it up:

copy each file to its new path  →  verify the copy (size and checksum)
→  switch the file rows together  →  delete the old copies

Rows switch only after every copy is verified. An old copy is deleted only when no row points to it and a verified copy exists at the new path.

3. Listings ask the database where to look. If a file's bytes haven't moved yet, the listing also checks the folder they're still in. A file is never hidden just because its bytes are in transit.

Designing for the half-done state

Background jobs crash eventually: a timeout, a deploy, a network blip. So everything rests on one rule: every file row always points to bytes that exist.

If the worker crashes... What's left behind What the next run does
While copying Rows at old paths, some copies made Skips finished copies, does the rest
Before switching rows Rows at old paths, all copies made Switches the rows
Before deleting old copies Rows at new paths, old copies remain Deletes them

There's no progress table to keep in sync. Each run works out what's left by comparing every file's storage path with its folder's path. A job that keeps failing ends up in a dead-letter queue (a holding queue for failed jobs) and raises an alarm, so nothing fails silently.

What it costs

  • Storage briefly holds two copies of every file being moved.
  • A folder can't be deleted while its files are still moving.
  • A browser tab opened before the switch may fail to open a file until it reloads.
  • One move has an estimated ceiling of 25,000 to 30,000 files. That's far above the largest folder today, but it's written down as a known limit.

Each of these is a deliberate trade for one guarantee: no file is hidden mid-move, and every row points to real bytes.

What I'd ask next time

When something "disappears" but wasn't deleted, look for two places that both think they own the same fact. Then ask:

  1. Which one is the source of truth? Make the other follow it.
  2. What does the user see while the change is half done? Design that state on purpose.
  3. What happens if it fails halfway? Make every step safe to run again.

The timeout was never the problem. It was where the problem showed up.

articles.title: AI Coding Tip 042 - Stop AI Cowboy Vibe Coding
articles.description: The spec asked for one change, and the AI shipped fourteen.   TL;DR: Reject any vibe-coded diff that...
articles.body_html:
The spec asked for one change, and the AI shipped fourteen.

TL;DR: Reject any vibe-coded diff that goes beyond the spec, and move the extras to their own case.

Common Mistake ❌

You ask the AI to fix one validation rule.

It fixes the rule, renames three variables, reformats the file, changes two unrelated rules, and rewrites a class nobody mentioned.

The tests pass and the vibes are good, so you send the pull request.

Your reviewer now reads a diff full of changes nobody asked for, and the real change hides inside it.

Good luck finding it.

That's vibe coding with no brakes.

It's also cowboy coding, and the AI finally made it affordable for everyone.

Another AI can do the same to the first one's work, with the same confidence.

Problems Addressed 😔

  • A reviewer can't tell the requested change from the extras, and the diff becomes a big pull request.

  • A defect in an unrequested change has no spec to blame, no ticket to trace, and no test written for it.

  • You can't revert the requested change without losing the unrequested ones.

  • A cleanup mixed with a behavior change hides regressions, the classic refactor with functional changes.

  • The spec stops being the source of truth, because the code does things nobody wrote down.

  • Approving a diff means approving decisions nobody discussed and agreed, which is an interesting way to run a team.

  • Every extra file adds merge conflicts for the rest of the team.

How to Do It 🛠️

  1. Write the change down before you prompt: the case description, the intention, the ticket, or the spec is the whole scope.

  2. List what's out of scope in the same document, and force the AI to obey it so it can't invent extras: no refactoring, no renames, no formatting, no new dependencies.

  3. Grant the AI write access only to the files the change needs, following least privilege.

  4. Ask the AI to plan first and list the files it'll touch, then compare that list with the scope.

  5. Send the diff to an adversarial reviewer: a different model in a fresh context that sees only the spec and the diff.

  6. Make the reviewer map every changed hunk to one numbered requirement, and flag each hunk it can't map.

  7. Point the reviewer at the tests the diff impacts, so it can measure the change: a test edited or deleted that the spec never mentioned, or a test outside the scope that now fails, shows the diff went too far.

  8. Wire that check into your harness as a criteria check that fails the task when any hunk is unmapped.

  9. Reject the pull request when the check flags unrelated hunks, and don't negotiate with it: every rejection is a finding you can turn into a rule.

  10. Cherry-pick the useful extras into a new case with its own spec, tests, and review, and put every refactoring there.

  11. Merge only when every hunk in the diff traces back to the spec.

Benefits 🎯

  1. Review the requested change: Your reviewer reads what someone asked for, and nothing else.

  2. Trace every line: Every hunk points to a requirement, so a defect has an owner and a ticket.

  3. Revert cleanly: You can back out one change without losing three others.

  4. Separate refactoring: A cleanup gets its own tests and its own review.

  5. Control other agents: The same check stops a second AI, or a teammate, from widening the change.

  6. Trust the spec: The code does what the spec says, and nothing more.

  7. Shrink the diff: A small pull request gets a real review instead of a skim.

  8. Measure the reach: The tests a diff impacts show how far it went, even when the code looks small.

  9. Keep changes proportional: A small functional change gets a small code change, so a big diff is a signal that something went wrong.

Context 🧠

Cowboy coding took effort once, and effort was a natural brake.

Now the AI sprawls in seconds, for anyone, human or agent.

Vibe coding means describing the goal and accepting the result with little close review.

Without a scope check, that's cowboy coding at machine speed.

The AI is a multiplier of the good and bad things.

Bertrand Meyer's modular continuity says a small change in the specification should trigger a small change in the code.

The bijection says it from the other side: the real world is the source of truth, and each thing in it has one object in the code.

articles.title: Why Your Android App Drops Frames: The Jetpack Compose Architecture Guide That Fixes Recomposition Forever
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into modern Android runtime architecture. Learn how the Compose Compiler SlotTable gap buffer works, why unstable types cause silent recomposition cascades, how to stop background Flow battery drain, and how to survive Android process death.
articles.body_html:
For years, Android development carried a reputation for boilerplate and ceremony.

You defined layouts in XML. You manually resolved view IDs with findViewById() or view binding. You synchronized widget states imperatively across Activities and Fragments. And if a single state mutation was missed, your UI fell into an inconsistent state with missing text, mismatched spinners, or phantom clicks.

Then Google delivered Jetpack Compose.

Compose promised to erase that legacy. Inspired by modern declarative paradigms, Compose allows developers to describe user interfaces purely as a function of state:

@Composable
fun UserProfile(user: UserState) {
    Column(modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp)) {
        Text(text = user.name, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleLarge)
        Text(text = user.bio, style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium)
    }
}

State changes, the UI updates automatically. No XML. No view binding. No manual view synchronization.

Developers embraced the transition. Teams rewrote entire feature sets in pure Kotlin. In simple test apps on flagship emulator devices, everything felt fluid and instant.

Then those apps shipped to real-world devices in production.

Users began reporting sluggish scrolling on LazyColumn lists. Frame rates on mid-range Android devices plummeted from a buttery 120Hz down to a stuttering 35Hz. Battery usage surged, and user reviews complained of mysterious battery drain when the app was minimized.

What happened?

The transition to declarative UI traded imperative view hierarchy management for a complex reactive runtime. When developers write Jetpack Compose without understanding its runtime mechanics, they accidentally trigger recomposition cascades, lambda instability, background coroutine leaks, and state loss during process death.

To build responsive, battery-friendly Android applications, you must look beneath the @Composable annotation.

Here is how Jetpack Compose and modern Android architecture actually execute.

1. The Core Engine: The SlotTable and Gap Buffer

A common misconception among web and mobile developers is that Jetpack Compose works like a Virtual DOM.

In React or Vue, changing state produces a tree of virtual nodes in memory. The runtime diffs the old virtual tree against the new virtual tree to calculate physical DOM mutations.

Jetpack Compose does not use a Virtual DOM. It uses a fundamentally different computer science data structure: the SlotTable backed by a Gap Buffer.

What Is the SlotTable?

The Jetpack Compose compiler is an official Kotlin compiler plugin. When it encounters a @Composable function, it intercepts the bytecode and rewrites the function signature, injecting a synthetic parameter called the Composer:

// What you write:
@Composable
fun Greeting(name: String)

// What the compiler produces in bytecode:
fun Greeting(name: String, $composer: Composer, $changed: Int)

The $composer parameter gives the function direct access to an internal array called the SlotTable.

The SlotTable is a flat, contiguous array that stores everything your Composable creates, remembers, or depends on. It contains:

  • The positional hierarchy of Composable calls.
  • Every value passed to remember { }.
  • State objects created by mutableStateOf().
  • Parameter values from the previous composition.

The Gap Buffer in Action

To update this flat array without expensive memory reallocations, the SlotTable employs a Gap Buffer, an ancient algorithm famously used in text editors like Emacs:

  1. The array contains a contiguous chunk of unallocated space called the Gap.
  2. When the compiler executes your Composable for the first time, it writes data sequentially into the array until it hits the Gap.
  3. When state changes and a sub-tree of Composables needs to update, the runtime moves the Gap to the current execution index in O(1) amortized time.
  4. New data is written into the Gap, and obsolete elements are overwritten without shifting the entire array.

Positional Memoization

This architecture powers remember.

When you write:

val formattedDate = remember(timestamp) {
    calculateExpensiveFormat(timestamp)
}

There is no dictionary or global hash map looking up timestamp.

Instead, the Composer inspects the current slot index in the SlotTable. It checks whether the stored slot contains the same timestamp value from the previous frame. If the value matches, it returns the cached result in a single array read. If timestamp changed, it re-executes the calculation, overwrites the slot, and stores the new value.

Because lookup is index-based rather than hash-based, positional memoization operates at raw CPU array access speeds.

2. The Stability Trap: Why Your Composables Keep Recomposing

If the SlotTable is so efficient, why do so many Jetpack Compose applications suffer from micro-stutters and dropped frames?

The primary culprit is Unnecessary Recomposition caused by Unstable Parameters.

Skippable vs Restartable

When the Compose compiler processes a @Composable function, it classifies it into two crucial behavioral categories:

  1. Restartable: The Composable can be re-executed when its inputs change or when state it reads mutates. Almost all non-inline Composables are restartable.
  2. Skippable: When a parent Composable recomposes, Compose can completely skip re-executing this child if all of its input parameters are proven to be unchanged.

If a Composable is not skippable, it re-executes every time its parent recomposes, even if its visible data has not changed a single pixel.

How the Compiler Infers Stability

How does the compiler decide if an input parameter is unchanged?

It inspects the type's Stability:

  • Primitive Types (Int, String, Boolean): Inherently Stable. Comparing old == new is trivial.
  • Functional Interfaces / Lambdas: Can be stable if they do not capture unstable local variables.
  • Classes with all val primitive properties: Marked Stable automatically.
  • Mutable Classes (var properties): Marked Unstable. The compiler cannot guarantee that internal properties did not mutate behind its back.

The Collection Trap (List<T> Is Unstable)

Here is the single most common performance trap in modern Android development:

@Composable
fun UserList(users: List<User>) {
    LazyColumn {
        items(users) { user ->
            UserRow(user = user)
        }
    }
}

You look at List<User> and assume it is immutable.

The Compose compiler disagrees.

In standard Kotlin, List<T> is an interface. A concrete implementation could easily be a mutable ArrayList<T> passed as a read-only interface reference. Because another thread could mutate the underlying array without changing the list reference, the Compose compiler marks standard Kotlin collections as Unstable.

The result?

Every time UserList receives an update, Compose cannot skip UserRow. If you have 50 items on screen and one item changes, Compose re-evaluates all 50 items from scratch.

The Fix for Unstable Collections

To restore skippability, you have two production solutions:

Solution 1: Kotlinx Immutable Collections

Use official immutable collection types that guarantee structural immutability:

import kotlinx.collections.immutable.ImmutableList

@Composable
fun UserList(users: ImmutableList<User>) {
    // Now 100% skippable!
}

Solution 2: The @Immutable Annotation

Annotate your UI state wrapper classes explicitly:

@Immutable
data class UserUiState(
    val users: List<User> = emptyList()
)

By adding @Immutable, you promise the Compose compiler that references will be treated as immutable, enabling skip optimizations across your entire component tree.

The Lambda Allocation Trap

Consider this button inside a list item:

@Composable
fun UserRow(user: User, onSelect: (String) -> Unit) {
    Button(onClick = { onSelect(user.id) }) {
        Text("View Profile")
    }
}

When UserList recomposes, the lambda { onSelect(user.id) } creates a brand-new object instance in heap memory on every frame.

Because the new lambda instance does not equal the old lambda instance, Button considers its inputs changed and forces a recomposition.

The Fix: Pass stable method references or use remember to stabilize the closure:

// Remembered lambda prevents allocation and maintains reference equality
val onUserClick = remember(user.id) {
    { onSelect(user.id) }
}
Button(onClick = onUserClick)

3. High-Frequency State: Taming derivedStateOf

What happens when your Composable observes a high-frequency state, like a scrolling list offset or a slider?

val listState = rememberLazyListState()

// NAIVE: Recomposes on every single pixel of scroll!
val showScrollToTopButton = listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 5

if (showScrollToTopButton) {
    ScrollToTopButton(onClick = { ... })
}

As the user scrolls, firstVisibleItemIndex and its underlying scroll offset update 60 to 120 times every second.

Evaluating a boolean condition directly in the Composable body forces the Composable to re-execute on every single pixel change, triggering severe UI jank.

The derivedStateOf Buffer

To decouple high-frequency inputs from low-frequency UI updates, Jetpack Compose provides derivedStateOf:

val listState = rememberLazyListState()

// OPTIMIZED: Only triggers recomposition when the boolean result flips
val showScrollToTopButton by remember {
    derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 5 }
}

derivedStateOf observes the high-frequency state internally without notifying the parent Composable. It only notifies the composition when the derived calculation actually changes its output value (e.g., from false to true).

Instead of recomposing 1,000 times during a continuous fling scroll, your Composable recomposes exactly once.

4. The Battery Vampire: Flow Collection and the Lifecycle Trap

Kotlin Coroutines and StateFlow are the modern standard for emitting reactive UI state from Android ViewModels.

However, bridging Kotlin Flows into Jetpack Compose contains one of the most dangerous battery drain pitfalls in the Android ecosystem.

// DANGEROUS: Wastes battery and leaks background work
@Composable
fun DashboardScreen(viewModel: DashboardViewModel) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsState()

    DashboardContent(state = state)
}

What is wrong with collectAsState()?

collectAsState() begins collecting the StateFlow when the Composable enters composition and continues collecting until it leaves composition.

Now imagine this scenario:

  1. The user opens your app. DashboardScreen begins collecting viewModel.uiState.
  2. The user presses the Home button. The app goes into the background.
  3. The Activity enters onStop(). The app is no longer visible on screen.

Because DashboardScreen is still in the composition hierarchy, collectAsState() continues collecting in the background.

If your StateFlow is backed by location updates, WebSocket streams, or database observers, your app continues executing background queries, processing JSON payloads, and burning device battery while sitting invisible in the user's pocket.

The Solution: collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

Google introduced the androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose library specifically to solve this problem:

import androidx.lifecycle.compose.collectAsStateWithLifecycle

@Composable
fun DashboardScreen(viewModel: DashboardViewModel) {
    // SAFE: Automatically pauses collection when app is in the background
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    DashboardContent(state = state)
}

Under the hood, collectAsStateWithLifecycle() wraps collection in repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED):

  • When the Activity transitions to STARTED, collection starts.
  • When the Activity drops to STOPPED (app backgrounded or covered by another app), the collection coroutine is instantly canceled.
  • When the user returns to the app, collection restarts automatically.

Never use raw collectAsState() in UI screens. Always use collectAsStateWithLifecycle().

5. Surviving the OS Assassin: Process Death vs Configuration Changes

One of the most persistent misconceptions among intermediate Android developers revolves around the ViewModel lifecycle:

"My state is stored in a ViewModel, so my user will never lose their data."

This statement is dangerously incomplete.

A ViewModel survives Configuration Changes (such as rotating the phone from portrait to landscape, or resizing a foldable screen). The Android runtime retains the ViewModel instance in memory while destroying and recreating the Activity.

However, a ViewModel does not survive Process Death.

What Is Process Death?

Android operates under aggressive memory constraints. When a user switches from your application to a memory-heavy game or the camera app, the Linux kernel's Low Memory Killer (LMK) needs RAM.

If your app is in the background, Android terminates your entire Linux OS process without warning:

[App in Background] ──► Low RAM Detected ──► Kernel Kills Process (SIGKILL)

When the user returns to your app via the recent apps switcher:

  1. Android starts a brand-new OS process from scratch.
  2. It recreates your Application and Activity classes.
  3. Your ViewModel is completely destroyed and re-instantiated with default values.

If the user was halfway through a multi-step checkout form, their filled fields, selected delivery options, and cart tokens are wiped clean, presenting a jarring blank screen.

The Contract of SavedStateHandle

To survive process death, your ViewModel must preserve critical session identifiers inside SavedStateHandle:

class CheckoutViewModel(
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle,
    private val repository: OrderRepository
) : ViewModel() {

    // Survives both configuration changes AND process death
    val orderId: StateFlow<String?> = savedStateHandle.getStateFlow("order_id", null)

    fun setOrder(id: String) {
        savedStateHandle["order_id"] = id
    }
}

SavedStateHandle serializes values into Android's low-level OS Bundle mechanism. When the process is assassinated, the operating system saves that tiny parcel in system server memory. When the process restarts, Android injects the preserved bundle right back into your ViewModel constructor.

The Golden Rule of State Persistence:

  • In-Memory Cache (ViewModel): Transient UI state, complex business objects, loaded list items.
  • SavedStateHandle: Navigation arguments, active IDs, entered text queries, selected tab indices (under 50 KB).
  • Persistent Disk (Room / DataStore): Full offline data, authentication tokens, user preferences.

6. Production Architecture: The Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) Blueprint

How do the highest-rated Android applications structure state to guarantee predictable rendering, zero recomposition cascades, and total testability?

They implement a strict Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) with immutable sealed state interfaces.

Here is a production-grade template:

// 1. Immutable State Definition
@Immutable
sealed interface ProductListUiState {
    object Loading : ProductListUiState
    data class Success(val products: ImmutableList<Product>) : ProductListUiState
    data class Error(val message: String) : ProductListUiState
}

// 2. Clear Intent / Event Modeling
sealed interface ProductListIntent {
    data class SelectProduct(val productId: String) : ProductListIntent
    object Refresh : ProductListIntent
}

// 3. Robust ViewModel
@HiltViewModel
class ProductListViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repository: ProductRepository,
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle
) : ViewModel() {

    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<ProductListUiState>(ProductListUiState.Loading)
    val uiState: StateFlow<ProductListUiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow()

    fun handleIntent(intent: ProductListIntent) {
        when (intent) {
            is ProductListIntent.Refresh -> loadProducts()
            is ProductListIntent.SelectProduct -> { /* Handle navigation */ }
        }
    }

    private fun loadProducts() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _uiState.value = ProductListUiState.Loading
            try {
                val data = repository.getProducts().toPersistentList()
                _uiState.value = ProductListUiState.Success(data)
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                _uiState.value = ProductListUiState.Error(e.localizedMessage ?: "Unknown error")
            }
        }
    }
}

Why This Architecture Wins:

  1. Single Source of Truth: State flows down; events flow up. The UI cannot mutate state directly; it can only emit intents.
  2. Deterministic UI Rendering: Using sealed interfaces guarantees that the UI can never accidentally display a loading spinner and an error message simultaneously.
  3. Immutable Collections: Wrapping data in ImmutableList enables the Compose compiler to skip recompositions on unchanged list rows with zero guesswork.

7. Ahead-Of-Time Performance: Baseline Profiles

Have you ever built a Jetpack Compose app, tested it on your physical phone, and felt disappointed by initial startup lag and slight stuttering during the first scroll?

Before panicking, check how you built the app.

In Debug mode, the Android runtime runs in interpreted JIT (Just-In-Time) mode with Compose tracking metadata enabled. Debug builds run up to 4x slower than production release builds.

However, even in Release mode, modern Android apps face an initial warm-up penalty because Android's Android Runtime (ART) must compile DEX bytecode into machine code as users interact with screens.

To eliminate this warm-up lag, Google introduced Baseline Profiles:

[Release APK] + [Baseline Profile Rules] ──► ART Pre-compiles Critical Code at Install Time ──► Instant 60-120Hz Scroll

A Baseline Profile is a text file bundled with your app that tells ART which classes and methods are critical for app startup and list scrolling. When the user downloads your app from Google Play, ART pre-compiles those exact Compose routines into machine code at install time.

Adding a Baseline Profile typically yields:

  • Up to 40% faster app startup times.
  • Immediate zero-jank frame rendering during the user's very first scroll.

The Mental Shift

Building high-performance Android apps in the modern era requires letting go of obsolete mental habits:

  • Stop thinking of UI as a tree of persistent XML views that you manually modify.
  • Jetpack Compose is a compiler-driven reactive engine powered by the SlotTable gap buffer.
  • Unstable parameters and raw List<T> types trigger silent, expensive recomposition storms.
  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle() protects user battery life when screens enter the background.
  • And ViewModels must be backed by SavedStateHandle to survive the operating system's Low Memory Killer.

Once you master these runtime mechanics, declarative Android development transforms from a mysterious, lag-prone struggle into one of the most expressive, resilient, and blazingly fast engineering platforms in software.

How has your team tackled recomposition optimization in Jetpack Compose? Have you run into stability surprises with Kotlin collections, or integrated Baseline Profiles into your release pipeline? Share your production experiences and architecture strategies in the comments below.

articles.title: Why Your AI Release Notes Hallucinate: The "Why vs What" Problem in Git History
articles.description: Passing raw git diffs to LLMs produces plausible but hallucinated changelogs. Here is why extracting the real "why" requires linked issues and counterfactual evals.
articles.body_html:
I once deployed an automated release pipeline that piped raw git diff outputs straight into an LLM prompt. Two hours later, our generated release notes claimed that version 1.4.0 "optimized JSON payload serialization for low-latency clients."

In reality, the underlying commit was an emergency patch for a memory leak that crashed Kubernetes pods under peak traffic. The code diff happened to delete several buffer allocations, and the model fabricated an appealing performance feature out of thin air.

That incident exposed a fundamental blind spot in how engineering teams automate changelogs with AI.

Commits Record the "What", Not the "Why"

When we ask an LLM to read a git commit or unified diff, we are asking it to divine human intent from syntax changes.

A diff tells you that timeoutMs changed from 5000 to 15000. It does not tell you that downstream payment gateways began dropping socket handshakes during cloud provider migrations. Without grounding context, the model resolves the ambiguity by inventing the most statistically plausible narrative: "improved network stability."

This becomes dangerous when breaking changes are involved. According to the Conventional Commits v1.0.0 specification, breaking changes can reside inside commit message footers or body paragraphs. A naive diff parser summarizes the altered function signature, while completely erasing the migration path requested by the engineer.

The Agent PR Trap: Slick but Unsupported Rationales

The problem deepens as more code is authored by autonomous AI coding agents. Agent-generated pull requests often arrive with beautifully formatted markdown descriptions. When I analyzed hundreds of these descriptions, I identified three recurring archetypes:

  1. Grounded intent: Accurately relays verifiable user and business motivations.
  2. Unsupported-plausible: A polished, convincing explanation that sounds authoritative but has zero backing in the actual issue or user bug report.
  3. Implementation-only: A dry walkthrough of AST changes without explaining user impact.

Standard summarization prompts routinely latch onto the unsupported-plausible archetype. The resulting changelog looks convincing to release managers, but distributes false technical claims to your users.

Mining Ground Truth from Linked Issues

To stop LLMs from hallucinating reasons, I re-engineered the extraction pipeline in @necoz-oss/changelog-bot (hosted on GitHub).

Instead of relying solely on PR descriptions or diffs, the engine tracks back to where the problem was originally defined: the linked GitHub issue. Under the GitHub Issue Linking specification, closing keywords establish verifiable causal links.

// Match GitHub closing keywords preceding an issue reference or URL.
// See: https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue
export const CLOSING_KEYWORD_PATTERN =
  /(?:\b(?:close[sd]?|fix(?:e[sd])?|resolve[sd]?))\s*[:：]?\s*(?:\[[^\]]+\]\((?<markdownUrl>https?:\/\/[^\s)]+)\)|(?<issueUrl>https?:\/\/[^\s)]+\/issues\/(?<urlIssueNumber>\d+)\b)|(?:(?<repoPrefix>[\w.-]+\/[\w.-]+)?#(?<issueNumber>\d+)))/gi;

export function resolveLinkedIssueNumbers(
  prBody: string,
  repo: { owner: string; repo: string },
): number[] {
  const matches = Array.from(prBody.matchAll(CLOSING_KEYWORD_PATTERN));
  const issueNumbers = matches
    .map((match) => match.groups?.issueNumber || match.groups?.urlIssueNumber)
    .filter(Boolean)
    .map(Number);

  return Array.from(new Set(issueNumbers)).slice(0, 2);
}

Mining issue context introduces network risk. To protect CI runners against GitHub API rate limits, I bounded issue resolution concurrency and implemented strict sanitization. Noisy stack traces and debug dumps are stripped before candidate snippets reach the evaluation step, falling back gracefully to heuristic summaries if the API degrades.

Naive Diff Summarizers vs. Grounded Release Pipelines

The differences between an ad-hoc AI prompt and a ground-truth pipeline determine whether your changelog can be trusted in production.

Architectural Dimension Naive Git Diff + LLM Prompt Grounded Pipeline (ChangelogBot Approach)
Primary Context Source Raw lines added and deleted Linked issue bodies and closing keywords
Noise Filtering Ingests raw stack traces and AST churn Sanitizes logs; bounds concurrent API requests
Hallucination Defense None (pure probability generation) Counterfactual calibration and archetype scoring
Delivery Decoupling Hardcoded to create PRs or write files Unix-compliant output (stdout, file, pull-request)
API Failure Fallback Hard CI build failure Graceful degradation to deterministic heuristics

Benchmarking with Counterfactual Evaluation

How do you verify whether an extractor captures genuine rationale rather than plausible fluff? You cannot rely on human intuition when reviewing hundreds of releases.

I built a counterfactual test corpus containing matched case families. For each pull request, the benchmark provides:

  • A verified rationale grounded in real user reports.
  • Counterfactual decoy rationales (plausible statements that describe unrelated features or false root causes).

By tracking the False Positive Rate (FPR) when the extractor is presented with decoy options, I could mathematically penalize models that pick convincing-sounding lies. If an extraction engine cannot consistently reject a counterfactual candidate, it has no place in an automated production release pipeline.

Decoupling Delivery for Safe CI Workflows

The final anti-pattern I eliminated was coupling changelog generation to write-heavy side effects.

Traditional tools halt your CI pipeline if you do not grant them a write-scoped GitHub personal access token to open a pull request. I restructured changelog-bot so that changelog generation is completely decoupled from delivery:

  • --output stdout: Emits clean, streamable release markdown to standard out, redirecting all telemetry and diagnostic logs strictly to stderr.
  • --output file: Appends updates locally to CHANGELOG.md with zero network overhead.
  • --output pull-request: Reserves write token requirements strictly for automated PR creation.

This separation means developers can test release notes locally or pipe them into custom release scripts without provisioning repository write access.

The Takeaway

  1. Stop summarizing diffs: Diffs tell you what changed in syntax; linked issues explain why the change mattered to users.
  2. Benchmark against decoys: Use counterfactual test sets to quantify whether your LLM can reject plausible but ungrounded claims.
  3. Keep delivery decoupled: Ensure your changelog generator can emit pure markdown to stdout without mandating write permissions.

What failure modes have you encountered when feeding git logs or PR descriptions into LLMs?
