articles.title: The Art of the Canary in the Age of AI
articles.description: Companion repository: copyleftdev/canary-article — full experiment, source code, run artifacts,...
articles.body_html:
Companion repository: copyleftdev/canary-article — full experiment, source code, run artifacts, and evidence explorer. All 30 main-attempt results are inspectable.

The first completed pilot run produced exactly the signal we had asked for:

CANARY:fd11c73f1ba333de

Then the agent explained that it couldn't access the project files or run checks. Our container was missing an execution helper, codex-code-mode-host. The requested feature had not been implemented.

The canary was present. The work could not proceed.

That was an infrastructure failure in our pilot, not a discovered booking bug or a result from the main experiment. The distinction became the first useful lesson of the project: a visible signal needs a precise meaning.

We preserved the failed pilot, documented the runtime defect, and started a replacement cohort after fixing it. You can inspect the original response, independent evaluation, and amendment.

The question behind the experiment survived: what does an instruction canary actually tell us about an AI coding agent's work?

A small signal with a long history

Mining canaries responded to dangerous gases before their human handlers did. One detail makes that history more interesting than the familiar metaphor: the Science Museum holds a canary cage equipped with an oxygen cylinder. Its design allowed a poisoned bird to be enclosed and given oxygen. Detection was connected to a response. Science Museum collection

Software borrowed the canary metaphor. A deployment canary exposes a limited population to a change and evaluates it against a control before a wider rollout. Google's SRE workbook describes both the rollout and the evaluation needed to make that useful. Canarying Releases

An instruction canary uses a different mechanism. We place a small requirement in project instructions and look for its observable effect: perhaps a recognizable word at the start of the agent's response.

That output proves something narrow: the response satisfied that particular requirement. Establishing a relationship to other behavior takes additional evidence.

This technique already has implementations. Context Canary displays a bird associated with a response marker and supports checkpoints distributed through instructions. Its documentation also explains that a missing marker does not prove context loss. Our contribution is a reproducible experiment that puts the marker beside independent checks of the resulting code.

Give the canary one clear job

Here is the instruction used in our marker condition, with an example token:

The first nonempty line of your final response must be exactly
CANARY:0123456789abcdef, with no other characters on that line.
Put all other text on subsequent lines.

It belongs in a project instruction file supported by the chosen coding tool. For Codex, AGENTS.md participates in a documented discovery chain with project and global scopes. Verify the applicable location and overrides for your tool; an instruction sitting on disk is not automatically evidence that it reached the model. Codex instruction discovery

Our runner generates a different token for every marker run. It puts that instruction in AGENTS.md, without repeating the token in the task prompt. The scorer checks the terminal final response, excluding tool output and intermediate messages.

We distinguish exact matches, malformed occurrences, absent tokens, and unobserved final responses. A timeout with no final response is not the same observation as a response that omitted its marker.

We also keep four questions separate:

  • What evidence shows that the instructions were loaded?
  • Did the final response satisfy the marker instruction?
  • Did the resulting code pass the specified behavioral checks?
  • Was the requested feature actually completed?

Instruction context and enforcement are different mechanisms. Anthropic makes that distinction explicitly in its memory documentation, which also describes loading diagnostics and hooks. How Claude remembers your project

Build something worth checking

Our experimental subject is a small Python booking module with two meeting rooms. It has no database, web server, or current-time dependency. That keeps the work small enough to inspect while giving mistakes a concrete meaning.

Its contract includes three important rules: reservations for the same room must not overlap; timestamps must carry an explicit offset and be normalized to UTC; rejected operations must leave existing bookings unchanged.

Adjacent reservations are allowed. Different rooms may be booked at the same time. These details are written down before the agent starts, because hidden checks should exercise a published contract rather than introduce surprise requirements.

Each run starts from the same working baseline and gets one task:

  1. Add rescheduling while preserving a booking's identity and room.
  2. Return the rooms available during a requested interval.
  3. Add a batch of reservations atomically, so one invalid member prevents the entire batch from being saved.

The fixture contract defines the API and edge cases. The tasks are independent; a later task does not inherit an earlier agent's implementation.

Test the measuring equipment

Before measuring agents, we calibrated the evaluator with 16 cases. They include correct implementations, deliberately broken overlap and timestamp handling, partial batch writes, missing features, import failures, and an import that hangs.

All 16 met their calibration expectations. That means the evaluator recognized the expected outcomes; it does not mean the deliberately broken programs passed the booking checks. For the hanging import, the expected outcome was a timeout with unevaluable behavior and verified container cleanup. These cases are test equipment validation, not model runs. Calibration record

The agent can see public examples. Evaluator-owned checks and reference implementations remain outside its container. After the agent stops, the saved submission runs in a separate evaluation container without network access or credentials.

This arrangement also keeps the agent's claim that tests passed separate from the evaluator's evidence. A feature can be missing even while the original baseline still passes its existing-operation checks—as our failed runtime pilot demonstrated.

After repairing that runtime, we completed six replacement pilot runs: one marker and one no-marker run for each task. All six passed their independent rule and feature checks; all three marker responses matched exactly. Those pilots checked that the procedure worked. They remain outside the main dataset. Replacement pilot report

Freeze the comparison before reading the result

The main plan contains 30 attempts: three tasks, two conditions, and five repetitions. Fifteen runs receive the marker instruction. The other fifteen receive the same project rules without it.

We randomize task/repetition blocks and the order of the two conditions within each block. Sessions and workspaces start fresh. This study uses Codex CLI 0.166.0, the gpt-6-astra model alias, high reasoning effort, and a 240-second limit per attempt. The saved plan records those settings, the runtime image, source hashes, and execution order. The underlying provider backend revision is unavailable, which limits exact model reproducibility.

We froze the plan before main collection. Failed attempts remain in the ledger rather than being silently retried or replaced. This is a local audit trail, not a public preregistration.

Thirty attempts are a small exploratory case study. Repeated calls to the same model do not establish independent samples, and hundreds of test assertions do not turn one agent run into hundreds of observations. Full protocol

The result was uniformly green

All 30 main attempts completed. Every submission built and passed both its feature-acceptance and project-rule checks. There were no main-study timeouts, interrupted attempts, missing final responses, or unevaluable results.

Task No marker: feature and rule checks passed With marker: feature and rule checks passed Exact markers
Rescheduling 5/5 5/5 5/5
Availability 5/5 5/5 5/5
Atomic batch booking 5/5 5/5 5/5

Among the fifteen marker-enabled runs, the table was equally simple:

Marker instruction Rule checks passed Rule checks failed
Exact match 15 0
Noncompliant marker 0 0

The fifteen no-marker controls do not belong in that second table. Their feature and rule outcomes remain in the first one. None of the marker runs were excluded for unavailable evidence. Complete main-study report

For a representative example, reschedule-01-B returned its exact marker and passed the independent checks. All fifteen marker-enabled runs shared that overall outcome.

This supports a narrow observation: the marker format was followed in every marker-enabled run in this setup. It does not establish the marker's value as a warning signal. We saw neither a marker omission nor a checked rule failure, so we cannot compare failure rates between compliant and noncompliant responses. The fraction of failures accompanied by a warning is undefined because there were no observed failures.

These were short edits to a working baseline that already supplied timestamp normalization and conflict-checking helpers. We did not test long-session drift or large architectural changes. Automatic instruction-loading diagnostics were unavailable, although pilot transcripts recorded explicit reads of AGENTS.md. We kept the fixed tasks and sample rather than increasing difficulty until a disagreement appeared. A study of warning lead time would need a different, longitudinal design.

Make the evidence easy to inspect

The companion project, Canary Lab, produces a standalone HTML report and machine-readable JSON. Each planned run stays visible. Marker status, feature completion, rule checks, and missing evidence have separate fields. The evidence explorer lets you filter by task or condition and expand a run's instructions, prompt, final response, code diff, and evaluation.

Saved submissions can be evaluated again without another model call. That makes the project useful beyond the article: readers can investigate a surprising result or adapt the contract to their own project. The run guide covers setup, calibration, pilots, collection, and replay.

What this study can and cannot tell you

This experiment produced a uniform-green result: 30/30 passed, 15/15 markers matched. That supports a narrow claim — the canary format is followable — but it invites the right challenges. Here are the ones I expect, and what the evidence actually says.

"You only tested short, isolated tasks." Correct. Each run is a fresh session with a single edit against a working baseline that already provides timestamp normalization and overlap helpers. Long-session drift, multi-turn state decay, and context-window pressure are not tested. The study would need a different, longitudinal design to measure those.

"You tested on a model that is too good to fail." Possible. We used gpt-6-astra with high reasoning effort. A weaker model might omit the marker more often — which is exactly where the canary DIAGNOSTIC value would appear. The uniform-green result means either the task was too easy or the model was too reliable. Both are genuine limitations, and the protocol is explicit about them.

"The canary proves nothing about code correctness." It does not. We keep four questions separate on purpose: instruction loading, marker compliance, behavioral checks, and feature completion. A present canary does not mean the feature was built correctly. An absent one means something is wrong upstream — but we had zero absent markers, so we cannot demonstrate that link.

"AGENTS.md might not have been loaded." For Codex, AGENTS.md participates in a documented discovery chain. Pilot transcripts recorded explicit reads of the file. Automatic loading diagnostics were not available at the time, so we cannot rule out a silent skip. A tool that exposes loading evidence would strengthen this.

"Correlation is not causation — even if a marker omission preceded a failure, that would not prove the omission caused it." True. A missing canary and a booking-rule failure could both be downstream of the same root cause (context loss, instruction collision, timeout). The canary is a diagnostic signal, not a causal proof. Its value is in making invisible failures visible so you can investigate.

"30 runs is not a study." It is a small exploratory case study. The n=30 does not establish independent samples (same model, same session structure), and 15 marker vs 15 control runs provide zero failures to correlate against. The companion project is built so anyone can run it with more models, harder tasks, or longer sessions and produce new evidence.

"The canary instruction itself could influence the agent's behavior." It could. The marker instruction occupies tokens in context. It might compete with the task instructions for attention. We did not measure an attention-budget effect. A study isolating that would need a control condition with an equal-length neutral instruction.

These are not weaknesses to hide behind caveats. They are the limits of what a 30-run single-model experiment can claim. The project is public precisely so someone else can push past these limits — with more models, longer sessions, harder tasks, and a result that breaks the streak.

What to do with an instruction canary in a real project

Start with one cheap, unambiguous marker and a specific question about instruction handling. Confirm how your tool loads it. Keep the marker easy to recognize and avoid treating a general “rules followed” statement as evidence for every rule.

Pair it with a check of the behavior you care about. If the concern is overlapping reservations, exercise overlapping reservations. If a requirement must hold at a particular tool boundary, consider an appropriate enforcement mechanism there.

Decide what an omission should prompt. Inspect loading diagnostics, check for conflicting instructions, re-establish the relevant requirement, and run its independent check. These are proposed engineering practices; this experiment does not compare recovery strategies or rank canary designs.

The craft is in matching a small signal to a question it can help answer—and keeping the evidence that answers the larger questions beside it.

articles.title: Cut Idle RAM on Fedora Linux: A Complete Service Controller, ZRAM Tuning & x86-64-v4 Compilation Guide
articles.description: Fedora Workstation is one of the best-engineered Linux desktops out there, but out of the box it...
articles.body_html:
Fedora Workstation is one of the best-engineered Linux desktops out there, but out of the box it ships like a Swiss Army knife built for every enterprise and consumer hardware scenario imaginable.

Even if you are running a modern single-NVMe laptop with no printer, no smartcard reader, no cellular modem, and no RAID array, Fedora quietly runs over a dozen background daemons, D-Bus watchers, and metadata pollers. Together, services like PackageKit, gnome-software, localsearch-3, abrt, colord, and cups routinely consume 600 MB to 1.2+ GB of idle RAM and trigger constant CPU wakeups that drain battery life.

Instead of running scattered systemctl commands that you will forget next week—or risking breaking system dependencies—I built a single, reversible Python CLI (service_control.py) to manage hardware services, reclaim RAM on demand, and toggle between Maximum Performance and Ultra-Battery modes without rebooting.

In this guide, we will cover:

  1. Which Fedora background services are safe to cut (and how much RAM they save).
  2. Kernel & ZRAM memory tuning to squeeze more multitasking headroom out of 8 GB and 16 GB laptops.
  3. How the controller works (mask vs. disable and state snapshots) + the complete drop-in source code.
  4. How to download source code and recompile apps with x86-64-v4 (AVX-512) on Fedora—including the real-world pros and cons.

1. What Gets Cut & How Much RAM You Reclaim

By default, systemd uses socket activation and D-Bus activation. Even if you run systemctl disable, another process can silently wake a daemon back up in the background. Using systemctl mask symlinks the unit to /dev/null, guaranteeing 0 MB RAM and 0% CPU until you explicitly unmask it.

Here are the safe, high-impact targets managed by the controller:

Target Key Systemd Unit(s) Scope What It Does & Why You Probably Don't Need It Typical RAM Saved
packagekit packagekit.service System Background DNF metadata daemon used by GNOME Software; locks DNF and eats huge RAM. 150 – 400 MB
indexer localsearch-3.service User Tracker/LocalSearch file content indexer; spikes CPU/disk I/O when downloading files. 80 – 250 MB
abrt abrtd, abrt-oops, abrt-xorg System Fedora's Automatic Bug Reporting Tool; constantly watches system journals for crashes. 40 – 90 MB
cups cups.service, .socket, .path System Local printing server; unnecessary if you rarely or never print. 25 – 60 MB
bluetooth bluetooth.service System Bluetooth stack and radio controller; keep masked when using wired peripherals. 15 – 30 MB
modem-manager ModemManager.service System Mobile broadband / cellular SIM hardware manager. 25 – 45 MB
color-profile colord.service System Display colorimeter & printer ICC profile daemon. 15 – 30 MB
avahi avahi-daemon.service, .socket System ZeroConf/mDNS local .local network discovery; reduces network wakeups on public Wi-Fi. 10 – 20 MB
geoclue geoclue.service System System-wide geolocation tracking service. 15 – 25 MB
usb-media gvfs-gphoto2, gvfs-afc, gvfs-mtp User Auto-mount watchers for digital cameras, iPhones, and MTP devices. 20 – 40 MB
smartcard gsd-smartcard.service User Corporate CAC / physical smartcard insertion watcher. 10 – 15 MB
wwan gsd-wwan.service User GNOME cellular WWAN settings daemon. 10 – 15 MB
stratis stratisd.service System Enterprise Stratis storage pool daemon (unused on Fedora's default Btrfs). 15 – 25 MB
dnf-poller dnf-makecache.timer / .service System Wakes up every few hours to download repository metadata in the background. Bandwidth + Wakeups
raid-check raid-check.timer / .service System Weekly software RAID array scrub (pointless on single-NVMe laptops). Disk I/O

Note: On top of these systemd units, killing the background gnome-software --gapplication-service resident process (handled automatically by the script's trim-ram command) immediately frees another 250 – 500 MB of RAM.

2. Beyond Services: Kernel, ZRAM & Power Optimizations

Cutting daemons is only half the story. Fedora uses ZRAM (a compressed block device in RAM) instead of a traditional disk swap partition. Many Linux users mistakenly apply old hard-drive swap tweaks (vm.swappiness=10), which actually hurts performance on ZRAM systems.

The upgraded controller includes a trim-ram command that applies three major memory and power optimizations:

  1. ZRAM-Optimal Kernel VM Tuning:
    • vm.swappiness=150: Encourages the kernel to compress cold, inactive anonymous pages into ZRAM early, leaving fast uncompressed RAM free for active applications and compilers.
    • vm.page-cluster=0: Disables swap read-ahead (which is designed for spinning HDDs, not zero-latency RAM).
    • vm.vfs_cache_pressure=50: Keeps filesystem directory/inode caches slightly longer so file searches stay snappy without ballooning memory.
  2. On-Demand PageCache & Bloat Purge (trim-ram):
    • Flushes dirty disk buffers (sync), drops clean kernel PageCache/dentries/inodes (/proc/sys/vm/drop_caches), and terminates resident gnome-software background processes before you launch a heavy workload.
  3. Instant Hardware Uncapping (uncap vs. cap):
    • Uses Fedora's native TuneD daemon (throughput-performance vs. powersave) alongside PCIe Active State Power Management (ASPM) (default vs. powersupersave) so your NVMe SSD and Wi-Fi card enter deep L1 sleep on battery, or run at zero bus latency when plugged in.

3. Architecture & Workflow Before You Copy the Code

Before dropping the script into your home directory, here is how it is structured so you never lock yourself out of hardware you actually need:

  • Zero Third-Party Dependencies: Uses only Python's standard library (sys, os, json, subprocess) and built-in Fedora tools (systemctl, tuned-adm, nmcli, upower, sysctl).
  • Smart State Snapshots (~/.service_control_state.json): When you run mask-all, the script records which services were originally active/enabled on your machine. Running unmask-all restores your exact prior state rather than blindly enabling daemons you never used.
  • Granular On-Demand Toggles: Need to pair Bluetooth headphones or print a document? Run enable bluetooth or enable cups, do your work, and run disable bluetooth when finished.

Daily Usage Examples 

# 1. Mask all redundant background daemons & timers
python3 ~/service_control.py mask-all

# 2. Check live service states and active TuneD profile
python3 ~/service_control.py status

# 3. Reclaim cached RAM, kill gnome-software bloat, and tune ZRAM VM params
python3 ~/service_control.py trim-ram

# 4. Inspect detailed RAM, ZRAM compression ratio, and top memory hogs
python3 ~/service_control.py ram

# 5. Uncap CPU Turbo Boost & disable PCIe sleep for compiling/gaming
python3 ~/service_control.py uncap

# 6. Switch back to Ultra-Battery mode & check live discharge wattage
python3 ~/service_control.py cap
python3 ~/service_control.py power

# 7. Temporarily re-enable Bluetooth when needed
python3 ~/service_control.py enable bluetooth

4. Complete Source Code: service_control.py

Save this file as ~/service_control.py and make it executable (chmod +x ~/service_control.py).

#!/usr/bin/env python3

    },
    "dnf-poller": {

    },

}


def run_cmd(cmd_list):
    """Executes a command quickly and returns (returncode, stdout, stderr)."""
    try:
        res = subprocess.run(cmd_list, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
        return res.returncode, res.stdout.strip(), res.stderr.strip()
    except Exception as e:
        return 1, "", str(e)


def get_unit_status(unit, scope):
    base_cmd = ["systemctl"]
    if scope == "user":
        base_cmd.append("--user")

    _, out, _ = run_cmd(base_cmd + ["is-active", unit])
    active = out if out else "unknown"

    _, out_en, _ = run_cmd(base_cmd + ["is-enabled", unit])
    enabled = out_en if out_en else "unknown"

    return active, enabled


def save_snapshot():
    """Saves pre-masking service states so unmask-all can restore accurately."""
    if os.path.exists(STATE_FILE):
        return
    snapshot = {}
    for key, info in SERVICES.items():
        snapshot[key] = {}
        for u in info["units"]:
            act, en = get_unit_status(u, info["scope"])
            snapshot[key][u] = {"active": act, "enabled": en}
    try:
        with open(STATE_FILE, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            json.dump(snapshot, f, indent=2)
    except OSError:
        pass


def load_snapshot():
    if not os.path.exists(STATE_FILE):
        return None
    try:
        with open(STATE_FILE, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except OSError:

  python3 ~/service_control.py uncap             # Max CPU/PCIe speed for compiling
  python3 ~/service_control.py cap               # Back to Ultra-Battery mode
  python3 ~/service_control.py enable bluetooth  # Turn on Bluetooth when needed
====================================================================================
""")


def cmd_uncap():
    print("\n🚀 Switching to MAXIMUM PERFORMANCE MODE (Uncapping)...")
    subprocess.run(["sudo", "-v"], check=True)

    run_cmd(["sudo", "tuned-adm", "profile", "throughput-performance"])

    aspm_path = "/sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy"
    if os.path.exists(aspm_path):
        subprocess.run(f"echo default | sudo tee {aspm_path} > /dev/null 2>&1", shell=True)

    print("✓ TuneD Profile: throughput-performance (Max Turbo Boost & low scheduler latency)")
    print("✓ PCIe ASPM: default (Zero bus sleep latency for NVMe & GPU)")
    print("✓ Status: UNCAPPED. System is running at MAXIMUM raw speed.\n")


def cmd_cap():
    print("\n🔋 Switching to ULTRA-BATTERY MODE (Capping)...")
    subprocess.run(["sudo", "-v"], check=True)

    run_cmd(["sudo", "tuned-adm", "profile", "powersave"])

    aspm_path = "/sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy"
    if os.path.exists(aspm_path):
        subprocess.run(f"echo powersupersave | sudo tee {aspm_path} > /dev/null 2>&1", shell=True)

    print("✓ TuneD Profile: powersave (Aggressive frequency downclocking at idle)")
    print("✓ PCIe ASPM: powersupersave (NVMe & Wi-Fi enter L1 deep sleep)")
    print("✓ Status: CAPPED. Maximum battery life active.\n")


def cmd_trim_ram():
    print("\n🧹 Running Deep RAM Reclamation & Fedora ZRAM Optimization...")
    subprocess.run(["sudo", "-v"], check=True)

    # 1. Flush dirty buffers and drop clean PageCache, dentries, and inodes
    run_cmd(["sync"])
    subprocess.run("echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches > /dev/null", shell=True)
    print("✓ Dropped clean Linux PageCache, dentries, and inodes.")

    # 2. Terminate resident gnome-software background service if running
    code, _, _ = run_cmd(["pkill", "-f", "gnome-software"])
    if code == 0:
        print("✓ Terminated resident gnome-software background process (~250-500 MB freed).")
    else:
        print("✓ gnome-software background process not running.")

    # 3. Apply Fedora ZRAM-optimized kernel virtual memory parameters
    vm_tweaks = {
        "vm.swappiness": "150",
        "vm.vfs_cache_pressure": "50",
        "vm.page-cluster": "0"
    }
    for param, val in vm_tweaks.items():
        run_cmd(["sudo", "sysctl", "-w", f"{param}={val}"])
    print("✓ Tuned ZRAM VM parameters (swappiness=150, page-cluster=0, vfs_cache_pressure=50).\n")


def cmd_ram():
    print("\n🧠 Live Fedora Memory & ZRAM Telemetry:")
    print("-" * 70)
    _, free_out, _ = run_cmd(["free", "-h"])
    print(free_out)

    print("\n📦 ZRAM Swap Device:")
    code, zram_out, _ = run_cmd(["zramctl"])
    print(zram_out if (code == 0 and zram_out) else "No active ZRAM device found.")

    print("\n⚙️ Kernel VM Parameters:")
    for param in ["vm.swappiness", "vm.vfs_cache_pressure", "vm.page-cluster"]:
        _, val, _ = run_cmd(["sysctl", "-n", param])
        print(f"  {param} = {val}")

    print("\n🔥 Top 5 RAM-Consuming Processes:")
    _, ps_out, _ = run_cmd(["ps", "-eo", "pid,rss,comm", "--sort=-rss"])
    for line in ps_out.splitlines()[:6]:
        parts = line.split(None, 2)
        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[1].isdigit():
            mb = int(parts[1]) / 1024
            print(f"  PID {parts[0]:<7} {mb:>7.1f} MB   {parts[2]}")
        else:
            print(f"  {line}")
    print("-" * 70 + "\n")


def cmd_fix_wifi():
    print("\n📶 Running Emergency Wi-Fi & Network Reset...")
    subprocess.run(["sudo", "-v"], check=True)

    run_cmd(["nmcli", "radio", "wifi", "off"])
    run_cmd(["sudo", "systemctl", "restart", "NetworkManager.service"])
    run_cmd(["nmcli", "radio", "wifi", "on"])

    print("✓ NetworkManager restarted.")
    print("✓ Wi-Fi radio reset and re-enabled.\n")


def cmd_power():
    print("\n⚡ Reading live battery power telemetry...")
    code, out, _ = run_cmd(["upower", "-i", "/org/freedesktop/UPower/devices/battery_BAT0"])
    if code == 0:
        for line in out.splitlines():
            if any(k in line for k in ["state", "energy-rate", "percentage", "time to empty", "voltage"]):
                print(" ", line.strip())
    else:
        print("Could not read battery device (on AC power or UPower unavailable).")
    print()


def cmd_status():
    print("\n" + "=" * 72)
    print(f"{'TARGET KEY':<16} {'SERVICE / TIMER NAME':<28} {'STATE':<12} {'MASKED?'}")
    print("=" * 72)
    for key, info in SERVICES.items():
        states = []
        masked_states = []
        for u in info["units"]:
            act, en = get_unit_status(u, info["scope"])
            states.append(act)
            masked_states.append("YES (Masked)" if en == "masked" else "No")

        main_act = states[0] if states else "unknown"
        main_mask = "YES (Masked)" if any("YES" in m for m in masked_states) else "No"

        act_display = f"\033[92m{main_act}\033[0m" if main_act == "active" else f"\033[90m{main_act}\033[0m"
        mask_display = f"\033[93m{main_mask}\033[0m" if "YES" in main_mask else main_mask

        print(f"{key:<16} {info['name']:<28} {act_display:<20} {mask_display}")

    _, profile, _ = run_cmd(["tuned-adm", "active"])
    print("=" * 72)
    print(f"Active Power Mode: {profile if profile else 'Unknown'}")
    print("=" * 72 + "\n")


def disable_target(key):
    if key not in SERVICES:
        print(f"Error: Unknown target '{key}'. Run 'python3 ~/service_control.py help' for valid targets.")
        return False

    info = SERVICES[key]
    scope = info["scope"]
    print(f"Stopping & masking {info['name']} ({key})...")

    for u in info["units"]:
        if scope == "system":
            cmd_stop = ["sudo", "systemctl", "stop", u]
            cmd_mask = ["sudo", "systemctl", "mask", u]
        else:
            cmd_stop = ["systemctl", "--user", "stop", u]
            cmd_mask = ["systemctl", "--user", "mask", u]

        run_cmd(cmd_stop)
        run_cmd(cmd_mask)

    print(f"✓ {info['name']} is now STOPPED and MASKED (0 MB RAM / 0% CPU).")
    return True


def enable_target(key, snapshot=None):
    if key not in SERVICES:
        print(f"Error: Unknown target '{key}'. Run 'python3 ~/service_control.py help' for valid targets.")
        return False

    info = SERVICES[key]
    scope = info["scope"]
    print(f"Unmasking & restoring {info['name']} ({key})...")

    for u in info["units"]:
        if scope == "system":
            cmd_unmask = ["sudo", "systemctl", "unmask", u]
            cmd_start = ["sudo", "systemctl", "start", u]
        else:
            cmd_unmask = ["systemctl", "--user", "unmask", u]
            cmd_start = ["systemctl", "--user", "start", u]

        run_cmd(cmd_unmask)

        # Only start unit if no snapshot exists OR it was originally active
        should_start = True
        if snapshot and key in snapshot and u in snapshot[key]:
            should_start = snapshot[key][u].get("active") == "active"

        if should_start:
            run_cmd(cmd_start)

    print(f"✓ {info['name']} is now UNMASKED and restored.")
    return True


def cmd_mask_all():
    print("\n>>> Activating Maximum Optimization Mode (Masking all redundant services & timers)...")
    subprocess.run(["sudo", "-v"], check=True)
    save_snapshot()

    for k in SERVICES.keys():
        disable_target(k)
    print("\n✓ All redundant background services & timers successfully masked!\n")


def cmd_unmask_all():
    print("\n>>> Restoring all managed services & timers back to default...")
    subprocess.run(["sudo", "-v"], check=True)
    snapshot = load_snapshot()

    for k in SERVICES.keys():
        enable_target(k, snapshot=snapshot)

    if os.path.exists(STATE_FILE):
        try:
            os.remove(STATE_FILE)
        except OSError:
            pass
    print("\n✓ All services restored!\n")


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        print_help()
        return

    action = sys.argv[1].lower().strip()

    if action in ["help", "-h", "--help"]:
        print_help()
    elif action == "status":
        cmd_status()
    elif action == "ram":
        cmd_ram()
    elif action == "trim-ram":
        cmd_trim_ram()
    elif action == "uncap":
        cmd_uncap()
    elif action == "cap":
        cmd_cap()
    elif action in ["fix-wifi", "wifi-fix", "reset-wifi"]:
        cmd_fix_wifi()
    elif action == "power":
        cmd_power()
    elif action in ["mask-all", "maskall", "disable-all"]:
        cmd_mask_all()
        cmd_status()
    elif action in ["unmask-all", "unmaskall", "enable-all"]:
        cmd_unmask_all()
        cmd_status()
    elif action in ["disable", "mask"]:
        if len(sys.argv) < 3:
            print("Error: Missing target name. Example: python3 ~/service_control.py disable packagekit")
            return
        disable_target(sys.argv[2].lower().strip())
    elif action in ["enable", "unmask"]:
        if len(sys.argv) < 3:
            print("Error: Missing target name. Example: python3 ~/service_control.py enable packagekit")
            return
        enable_target(sys.argv[2].lower().strip())
    else:
        print(f"Unknown command: '{action}'")
        print_help()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

5. Taking Speed Further: Compiling Apps with x86-64-v4 & AVX-512 on Fedora

Once you have freed up RAM and uncapped your CPU with python3 ~/service_control.py uncap, you might notice one more bottleneck: generic binary compilation.

Official Fedora RPM packages are compiled against the baseline x86-64 instruction set (dating back to 2003) so that a single binary runs on every 64-bit processor ever built. That means your modern processor's 512-bit SIMD vector engines (AVX-512) sit completely idle in most standard packages.

Step 1: Verify Your CPU Supports x86-64-v4

x86-64-v4 is the microarchitecture feature level that mandates AVX-512F, AVX-512BW, AVX-512CD, AVX-512DQ, and AVX-512VL (supported on AMD Zen 4 / Zen 5 Ryzen 7000/8000/9000 series and Intel 10th/11th Gen Ice Lake / Tiger Lake & Xeon Scalable CPUs).

Check support directly via Fedora's dynamic linker:

/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --help | grep x86-64-v

If you see x86-64-v4 (supported, searched) in the output, your CPU is ready.

Step 2: Download Source & Compile with x86-64-v4 Optimizations

You have two clean ways to build optimized binaries on Fedora:

Option A: Rebuilding a Fedora Source RPM (rpmbuild)

Ideal for system tools, libraries, ffmpeg, zstd, or Python interpreters:

# 1. Install Fedora RPM build tools and C/C++ compilers
sudo dnf install -y fedora-packager rpmdevtools gcc gcc-c++ clang make cmake

# 2. Set up the rpmbuild directory tree in ~/rpmbuild
rpmdev-setuptree

# 3. Download the source RPM for your target package (example: zstd)
dnf download --source zstd

# 4. Install its build dependencies and unpack the source
sudo dnf builddep -y zstd-*.src.rpm
rpm -ivh zstd-*.src.rpm

# 5. Build with x86-64-v4 + AVX-512 flags injected into RPM optflags
rpmbuild -ba ~/rpmbuild/SPECS/zstd.spec \
  --define "optflags -O3 -march=x86-64-v4 -mtune=native -pipe"

Your newly compiled, AVX-512-accelerated RPMs will be waiting in ~/rpmbuild/RPMS/x86_64/, ready to install with sudo dnf reinstall ~/rpmbuild/RPMS/x86_64/*.rpm.

Option B: Compiling Upstream C/C++ Projects Directly

For local AI engines (llama.cpp), media encoders, or scientific tools:

git clone [https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp.git](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp.git)
cd llama.cpp

cmake -B build \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-O3 -march=x86-64-v4 -mtune=native" \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-O3 -march=x86-64-v4 -mtune=native"

cmake --build build -j$(nproc)

6. Pros & Cons of x86-64-v4 / AVX-512 Compilation

Before recompiling your entire system, weigh where it actually shines versus where it hurts:

Pros

  • Massive Speedups in Vectorized Workloads (15% – 50%+): Video transcoding (FFmpeg / x265), local LLM CPU inference (llama.cpp), scientific math (NumPy / OpenBLAS), image processing, and zstd compression process 512 bits of data per clock cycle instead of 128 or 256 bits.
  • Double the Vector Registers: x86-64-v4 unlocks 32 wide ZMM registers (up from 16 YMM registers in AVX2), drastically reducing register spills to RAM inside tight loops.
  • Zero Runtime Dispatch Overhead: Many upstream binaries rely on runtime CPU feature detection; compiling natively eliminates branching overhead.

Cons

  • AVX-512 Frequency Downclocking & Heat (Intel Laptops): On Intel 10th/11th Gen laptops, heavy sustained 512-bit instructions draw significant current, causing the CPU to lower its all-core boost clock and ramp up fans. (Note: AMD Zen 4 and Zen 5 CPUs execute AVX-512 without severe clock penalties, making x86-64-v4 a pure win on modern Ryzen laptops).
  • Zero Binary Portability: A binary compiled with -march=x86-64-v4 will immediately crash with SIGILL (Illegal instruction) if copied to an older PC or a standard cloud VM that lacks AVX-512.
  • Minimal Gains for General UI/Web Apps: Browsers, file managers, and text editors are bottlenecked by memory latency, network I/O, and GPU compositing—not SIMD math. Save x86-64-v4 compilation for compute-heavy tools rather than wasting hours recompiling your desktop environment.
  • Manual Update Maintenance: Custom-compiled RPMs or binaries won't automatically receive DNF security patches unless you rebuild them when upstream updates drop.

Wrapping Up

Combining service masking, ZRAM-aware kernel tuning, on-demand TuneD uncapping, and targeted x86-64-v4 compilation turns Fedora into a lean, ultra-responsive workstation without sacrificing stability—and everything remains 100% reversible with a single command.

If you have other Fedora services or kernel sysctl tweaks in your daily toolkit, drop them in the comments!

articles.title: I store face embeddings in a hand-rolled write-ahead log, and it works great
articles.description: A few months ago I started building FaceMark, an attendance system that recognizes students' faces. A...
articles.body_html:
A few months ago I started building FaceMark, an attendance system that recognizes students' faces. A NestJS API handles auth, courses and attendance records, and a small FastAPI service runs DeepFace/TensorFlow to turn face photos into 512-dimensional embedding vectors and match them.

The AI service needs to persist those embeddings. My first version did what every tutorial does: a Python dictionary, pickled to a file.

It worked, right up until I thought about it for five minutes:

  • Every save rewrote the entire file. One crash mid-write and I lose every registered face.
  • No integrity checks. A corrupt byte somewhere means pickle.load explodes and I find out at 8 AM when a classroom full of students is waiting.
  • No deletes. Removing a student meant loading everything, popping a key, and rewriting everything.

I could have reached for SQLite, Redis, or a vector database. For the actual scale of this problem (a few thousand embeddings, writes only when a new student registers) all of them felt like operating a forklift to move a bookshelf. What I wanted was exactly the thing from Chapter 3 of Designing Data-Intensive Applications: an append-only log with an in-memory index, the Bitcask model. So I built it. It's about 200 lines of Python and it's been boringly reliable ever since.

The record format

Every record in the log is:

[CRC32: 4B][Timestamp: 8B][Tombstone: 1B][KeyLen: 2B][ValLen: 4B][Key][Value]

19 bytes of header, then the raw key and value. Keys are student IDs, values are JSON-encoded embedding vectors.

Writes are the simplest possible thing: seek to the end of the file, append the record, fsync, and update two in-memory structures — a keydir mapping each key to its (offset, size, timestamp) in the file, and a hot cache holding the actual vectors:

self._file.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
offset = self._file.tell()
self._file.write(record)
self._file.flush()
os.fsync(self._file.fileno())

self._keydir[key] = (offset, len(record), ts)
self._cache[key] = embedding

No seeking, no in-place updates, no locks to reason about. The file only ever grows.

Why the CRC32 earns its 4 bytes

The header starts with a CRC32 checksum over the rest of the record. On startup the engine scans the log sequentially and rebuilds the keydir and cache. If it hits a truncated record (the classic "process died mid-write" case) it stops there and discards the tail. If a record's CRC doesn't match, it logs the offset and skips it:

expected_crc = zlib.crc32(raw_header_payload + raw_payload) & 0xffffffff
if crc != expected_crc:
    print(f"[DDIA-WAL] Error: CRC mismatch at offset {offset}")
    corrupt_records += 1
    continue

This is the whole point of the exercise: a crash can cost me at most the tail of the file, never the whole store, and I always know exactly which record was lost. With the pickle file, the answer to "how much did I just lose?" was "yes."

Deletes are just more appends

You can't erase bytes from an append-only log, so deletes append a tombstone record — same format, tombstone flag set, empty value. During recovery, a tombstone removes the key from the index:

if tombstone == 1:
    self._keydir.pop(key, None)
    self._cache.pop(key, None)

Compaction keeps the file honest

Appending forever means superseded records pile up: every re-registered face and every tombstone is dead weight. Compaction writes only the currently-live records to a temporary file, then atomically renames it over the old log:

self._file.close()
os.replace(compact_path, self.wal_path)
self._file = open(self.wal_path, "a+b")
self._recover()

os.replace is atomic on both POSIX and Windows, so a crash during compaction leaves either the old file or the new one fully intact — never a half-written mix.

Reads and the actual workload

Face recognition needs every embedding to compare a camera frame against, so all_embeddings() just returns the in-memory cache — the comparison loop never touches disk at all. Single-key get checks the cache first, falls back to a keydir lookup, one seek and one read.

This is the part where the "just use a database" objection is fair, so let me be honest about the tradeoffs:

  • Everything lives in RAM. Fine for thousands of 512-float vectors, wrong for millions.
  • Single writer. There is no concurrency control because my workload has exactly one writer.
  • fsync on every write is slow. My writes happen a few times per day, so I happily pay milliseconds for durability.
  • Similarity search is brute-force linear scan. At this scale numpy does it faster than I can blink. When it stops being fast, that's a good problem to have, and the WAL still works as the persistence layer under a proper index.

The migration escape hatch

One detail I'm glad I added: on first run, if no WAL exists but the old pickle file does, the engine converts every record into WAL format before opening the store. Existing deployments upgrade themselves with zero drama.

What I got out of it

Building this taught me more about storage than a month of reading would have. Record framing, checksums, tombstones, atomic rename, crash recovery — these stopped being vocabulary and became code I had to get right. The full implementation is in the FaceMark repo (ai-service/wal_engine.py) if you want to pick it apart: https://github.com/ZiadtahaM/FaceMark

If you're storing something small, written rarely, and read constantly, and you're about to spin up Redis for it, maybe spend an afternoon with DDIA chapter 3 first.

articles.title: Saving Every Sixty Seconds Is Not Saving Your Work
articles.description: At 00:09:44 the timer saved. At 00:09:50 the third fix finished. Six seconds.  That is the whole...
articles.body_html:
At 00:09:44 the timer saved. At 00:09:50 the third fix finished. Six seconds.

That is the whole story, and everything below is me measuring what those six seconds cost. The timer saved a patch that did not have the third fix in it. The kill came at 00:10:19, before the next tick, and the window that held the finished, tested fix is gone. The fix was done. It was green. It is not in the patch, and there is no way to get it back except doing it again.

itsvicmoreno asked the question that made me run this. Under the last piece, the one about saving the patch after every step, he asked what happens if you save on a timer instead. A patch every sixty seconds, not after each step. On a longer job, how much does the timer version leave behind when the work dies between saves? I told him I would try it. Then he came back with a second point, and it is the sharper one: on a repo-wide rename, save before the test run, not after, because a test run that hangs takes the patch with it. So this run tests both. Same job, two ways of saving, a rename in the middle, and I killed the work myself both times so the kill point was not chosen to flatter either side.

The job was a small cart helper, ten steps. Nine one-line fixes, the kind where you read the failing test, change one line, and watch it go green, plus one rename in the middle where a function changes its name across two files. Twelve tests, two passing at the start, ten failing. Each step took about twenty seconds of reading and checking, so the whole job runs a few minutes, which is the point. The last piece proved the shape on a two-line fix. A two-line fix does not have enough room between saves for a timer to miss anything. Ten steps does.

The first version saved the patch after every step, the same shape as the last piece. Fix the line, save the patch, run the tests, write the result down, move on. I killed it at 144 seconds, in the middle of step six, before that step's edit had even started. Five steps were done and all five were in the patch. Getting back to green from a fresh copy took 2.17 seconds: take the template, apply the patch, run the tests. Eight of twelve tests passing, and the recovered file was identical to the one in the dead window, byte for byte. Nothing about the recovery depended on the window still being alive, because nothing about the saving did either.

The second version saved on a sixty-second timer and nothing else. Same ten steps, same pace. A background save every sixty seconds, no save after a step, no matter how finished the step was. I killed it at 95 seconds, in the middle of step five. Four steps were done. Four steps had been tested and were green. The patch had two of them.

Here is what that looks like, as numbered problems, because each one is a different way the timer fails.

  1. The timer loses finished work, and finished is the wrong word for what it loses. Steps three and four were not half done. Step three changed a line that added price and quantity instead of multiplying them. Step four changed a discount that subtracted the percent number instead of taking a percentage off. Both were edited, both were tested, both were green, both are in the test log I kept. The patch has neither. The work the timer lost is not the work in progress. It is the work you already finished and already proved, which is worse, because that is the work you stop thinking about. Step three missed the save by 5.9 seconds. Not a minute. Six seconds.

  2. The two records disagreed, and the wrong one looked healthier. The test log said seven of twelve passing. The patch said five. If you only read the log, you would think you had four steps banked. You had two. A log is a diary. A patch is the work. On the per-edit version the two always agreed, because the save and the test happened in the same step. On the timer version they drift apart by up to sixty seconds, and the drift is silent. Nothing warns you. The next tick would have fixed it, and the next tick never came.

  3. The timer's gap is bounded, and the bound is the wrong comfort. Sixty seconds is the most it can lose, and that sounds small until you ask what you can finish in sixty seconds. Two steps, in this run, forty-two seconds of green-tested work. On a real job, an hour of steps fits between the same two ticks if the kill lands late in the interval, and the interval does not care how much you did. It only cares when the clock says save. The bound is real. It bounds the wrong thing. It bounds time, and what you lose is work.

  4. The rename is where itsvicmoreno's second point lands, and it landed harder than I expected. The two random kills both fell before step seven, so the rename never ran in either main arm. I ran the timer version a third time and killed it right after the rename finished, to get the measurement. The rename took 26.31 seconds, the longest step in that run, and the patch was saved before the test run started. I can show the order in the timestamps: the patch file was written at 00:14:02, the test result was logged after it. If that test run had hung, the rename would already have been on disk. That is the whole rule. A rename touches two files and the test run after it is the one that can sit there forever, so the save goes before the test, not after it. In the timer version, that save is the only save that is not on the clock, and it is the only reason the rename survived. The timer would have caught it at the next tick, maybe. Maybe is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

The comparison, in one table:

Save after each step Save every 60 seconds
Kill point 144 s, mid-step 6 95 s, mid-step 5
Steps finished before the kill 5 4
Steps in the patch 5 2
Steps lost 0 2 (steps 3 and 4)
Recovery time 2.17 s 3.11 s
Tests passing after recovery 8 of 12 5 of 12

The recovery times are nearly the same, and that is worth saying plainly, because it is not where the difference lives. Applying a patch is cheap either way. The difference is what is in the patch when you apply it. The per-edit version recovered everything it had finished. The timer version recovered half of what it had finished, and the half it lost was the half it had finished most recently, which is the half you remember worst when you sit down to redo it.

The redo is the part nobody prices. Steps three and four are each one line. Typing them again takes seconds, and that is the number people quote when they say the timer is fine. But the redo is not the typing. It is remembering which two lines, out of ten, were the ones that did not make it. The test log says four steps were done and green. The patch says two. You have to work out which two are missing, and the only way to do that is to read the log against the patch line by line, then run the tests again to prove the retyped lines are the same ones. On this toy the whole thing takes a minute. On a real job the missing steps are not two lines with labels on them. They are the hours you spent finding the right line, and the only record of which line it was is a log entry that says it passed. The timer does not just lose the edit. It loses the proof that the edit was the right one, and the proof is the expensive part.

One more number, because itsvicmoreno asked for it and the last piece could not give it to him. The longest single step across all three runs was 46.23 seconds, step two of the per-edit version. It was not the edit. The edit was one line, the same as every other step. It was the test run going slow that once, about twenty-seven seconds against two to four for every other step's test run, for no reason I could find. That is the honest answer to his question, and it is also the reason the timer loses: the step that eats the interval is never the step you planned for. The rename, the step he was asking about, took 26.31 seconds. The slow test took 46. So if you are counting on a sixty-second gap being small, remember that one slow test run is most of it.

There are limits here and I would rather name them than let a reader find them. One random kill per version is two draws, not a distribution. The gap of two lost steps is what this draw produced. What carries over is the shape, not the count: a timer loses everything since the last tick, and the last tick is never when you need it. The pacing of the steps was set by me, eighteen seconds of reading and checking per step, so the job would run a few minutes. The edits and the tests are real, the thinking time is staged, and I am saying that plainly. The kill was staged by me in all three runs, and the reason a real stall happens stays unknown in a way my staged kill does not capture. And the recovery times are seconds because the test suite is twelve tests. On a real repo the seconds grow. The steps do not come back with them.

So here is the claim, and it is the one you can argue with: saving every sixty seconds is not saving your work. It is betting that nothing kills the work in the sixty seconds after you finish a step, and the bet gets worse the more steps you finish, because each finished step is another thing the next tick has not seen yet. Save after the step. Save the rename before the test. The timer can stay, as a backstop, but a backstop is not a plan.

What do you save, and when? If you have a timer running, has it ever actually saved you, or has it only ever saved most of you? And what is the longest single step you have watched eat a whole interval, a test run that would not finish, a rename across more files than you expected? I want the numbers, not the theory. The theory I already had. The theory said sixty seconds was fine.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: AI Coding Agents Raised Code Output 30% and Slowed PR Reviews 49%: How to Fix the Queue
articles.description: Two large-scale 2026 empirical studies reached the same answer on AI coding agents: drafting code got...
articles.body_html:
Two large-scale 2026 empirical studies reached the same answer on AI coding agents: drafting code got dramatically faster, while shipping finished software barely moved because human code review became the choke point. In a Harvard working paper covering over 700 firms, AI coding agents raised lines of code by 30% and pull requests by 23%, yet average PR submission-to-merge time jumped 49%.

What the two multi-tool studies actually measured

Both papers track real production engineering telemetry across multiple coding tools instead of synthetic benchmark tasks.

Harvard economists Fiona Chen and James Stratton (author research page, reported in detail by Ars Technica) analyzed 300 million work events across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 software companies through March 2026, later expanding the dataset to 445M work events across 720,542 workers at 655 firms. Across adopting companies, AI coding agents lifted lines of code by 30%, commits by 20%, and pull requests by 23%. Resolution rates for Jira issues and epics showed no statistically significant increase.

A separate NBER working paper (w35275) by Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff, and Liyuan Yang tracked more than 500,000 GitHub developers with AI usage telemetry. Cumulative commits rose 30% for autocomplete, 180% for interactive coding agents, and 240% for autonomous coding agents. Moving up the delivery funnel, that 240% commit gain dropped to 80% for projects and fell all the way to 30% for actual releases.

Empirical dataset Code generation gain Shipped output impact Measured bottleneck
Harvard / Jellyfish (over 700 firms, 700,000+ workers; expanded to 445M events across 655 firms) +30% lines of code, +20% commits, +23% pull requests No statistically significant rise in Jira issues or epics resolved +49% PR submission-to-merge time, +35% comments per PR, change requests nearly doubled
NBER w35275 (500,000+ GitHub developers) +30% commits (autocomplete), +180% (interactive), +240% (autonomous agents) +240% commit surge drops to +80% projects and +30% actual releases 0.23 elasticity of substitution between AI and human effort

The NBER authors tie this drop to the weak-link effect: an estimated elasticity of substitution of 0.23 between AI and human effort means faster drafting cannot substitute for human verification and review.

Why AI code reviewers did not clear the backlog

Teams already tried throwing automated review bots at the queue. In the Harvard dataset, 80% of measured firms had adopted some form of AI code review by March 2026. Even with broad adoption, AI generated only 23.3% of review comments across 10.8% of pull requests. Meanwhile, the share of human workers doing code reviews still climbed 14%.

The numbers point to two stacked failure modes. First, agents push 23% more pull requests into a fixed pool of senior maintainers who understand the codebase. Second, first-pass draft quality drops, so reviewers spend more cycles catching edge cases and sending work back, driving a 35% jump in comments per PR and nearly doubling the share of pull requests with changes requested.

Fixing the queue takes process gates before a human ever gets notified, not another bot leaving style comments after a reviewer is already paged.

Gate 1: Audit merge tail latency and change-request loops in your own repo

Before changing team rules, measure both median and 90th-percentile merge hours alongside review churn on your own merged pull requests. The GitHub CLI gh pr list manual exposes createdAt, mergedAt, reviews, and reviewDecision directly as JSON.

Pipe the last 50 merged PRs into a short Python check to measure median merge time, 90th-percentile tail wait, median review events, and how often drafts bounce back with CHANGES_REQUESTED (GitHub Pull Request Reviews REST docs):

gh pr list --state merged --limit 50 \
  --json number,createdAt,mergedAt,reviews,reviewDecision \
  | python3 -c '
import json, statistics, sys
from datetime import datetime

prs = json.load(sys.stdin)
merge_hours, rev_counts = [], []
changes_requested = 0

for pr in prs:
    created = datetime.fromisoformat(pr["createdAt"].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    merged = datetime.fromisoformat(pr["mergedAt"].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    merge_hours.append((merged - created).total_seconds() / 3600)
    revs = pr.get("reviews") or []
    rev_counts.append(len(revs))
    if any(r.get("state") == "CHANGES_REQUESTED" for r in revs):
        changes_requested += 1

merge_hours.sort()
p90 = merge_hours[int(0.9 * (len(merge_hours) - 1))]
print(f"Merged PRs analyzed: {len(prs)}")
print(f"Median hours to merge: {statistics.median(merge_hours):.1f}h")
print(f"90th-percentile hours to merge: {p90:.1f}h")
print(f"Median review events per PR: {statistics.median(rev_counts):.1f}")
print(f"PRs with CHANGES_REQUESTED: {changes_requested}/{len(prs)} ({100 * changes_requested / max(len(prs), 1):.1f}%)")
'

Running that exact command against the last 50 merged pull requests on modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk produces:

Merged PRs analyzed: 50
Median hours to merge: 0.4h
90th-percentile hours to merge: 44.1h
Median review events per PR: 2.0
PRs with CHANGES_REQUESTED: 0/50 (0.0%)

Looking only at the 0.4h median would suggest there is no queue at all, while the 44.1h 90th-percentile merge time reveals where harder PRs actually stall. Running the same snapshot weekly before and after changing PR rules shows whether your backlog sits in queue wait or in repeated revision rounds.

Gate 2: Force every agent PR into Draft mode so CODEOWNERS stay quiet until CI passes

Most review queues clog because an agent finishes a loop and opens a normal pull request immediately, paging every owner before tests finish or the author inspects the diff. Under GitHub's CODEOWNERS rules, code owners are not automatically requested to review draft pull requests. When you mark a draft pull request as ready for review, code owners are automatically notified.

Make Draft mode the default in your agent prompt instructions and shell workflow using gh pr create --draft and gh pr ready:

# 1. Agent opens every PR as a draft so CODEOWNERS are not paged on broken runs
gh pr create --draft --fill

# 2. Only after local tests, CI checks, and author diff inspection pass:
gh pr ready

That single change keeps raw agent output out of senior engineers' notification queues while the author trims dead code, verifies edge cases, and fixes failing checks.

Gate 3: Block ready-for-review PRs that lack a reproducible verification block

Draft mode protects reviewer attention during CI, while a pre-review workflow stops half-baked drafts from triggering change-request loops after they turn ready. Using GitHub Actions pull_request triggers for opened, synchronize, and ready_for_review, require every non-draft PR to pass tests and include a non-empty verification section describing the exact command run to prove behavior:

name: PR Review Readiness Gate

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, ready_for_review]

jobs:
  verify-before-human-review:
    if: github.event.pull_request.draft == false
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Check PR verification block
        env:
          pr_body: ${{ github.event.pull_request.body }}
        run: |
          python3 - << 'PY'
          import os, re, sys
          body = os.environ.get("pr_body", "")
          match = re.search(r"(?is)##\s+Verification\s*\n(.+)", body)
          if not match or len(match.group(1).strip()) < 25:
              print("Missing ## Verification section with test command and observed result.")
              sys.exit(1)
          print("Verification block present.")
          PY
      - name: Run full test suite
        run: npm test

Because the job skips draft pull requests (github.event.pull_request.draft == false) and fires automatically on ready_for_review, authors and agents can iterate freely in draft while guaranteeing that any PR reaching a human reviewer has both green tests and a written verification trace.

Keep review capacity ahead of drafting speed

Faster code generation only raises shipped output when review capacity and draft verification scale with it. Measure your current tail merge latency and CHANGES_REQUESTED rate with gh pr list, default agent PRs to --draft so CODEOWNERS are only notified on verified work, and run a ready_for_review readiness gate before human reviewers open the diff.

Where has the review queue slowed down most on your repositories since adopting coding agents, and which workflow change actually cut back the revision loops?

articles.title: One Script, Four Documents
articles.description: The rules were already knowable, so I didn't put a model in the pipeline.  A video course may begin...
articles.body_html:
The rules were already knowable, so I didn't put a model in the pipeline.

A video course may begin with one master script, but the people producing it rarely need the same document. The presenter needs clean narration for a teleprompter. The screencast recorder needs actions, commands, visual cues, and voiceover. The motion designer needs animation instructions. The producer needs an overview of the videos, their components, and approximate runtimes.

Maintaining those as four independent documents creates a familiar problem. The moment the script changes, someone has to remember every downstream copy. A corrected line of narration might reach the presenter but not the producer. A revised demonstration might appear in the recording instructions but not the production plan. The documents are all plausible, yet they no longer describe the same course.

I've run into versions of this coordination problem for years, building curriculum at MongoDB University and working with developers through Cisco DevNet, and I wanted to try something different: treat the master production script as structured source material, validate it, and generate the role-specific documents deterministically. Instead of asking people to reconcile several copies, make the copies products of the same source.

I built the experiment around a fictional course, Understanding APIs: A Winery's Digital Cellar. The winery setting was a convenient way to make an API course approachable, and I enjoy projects where the example has a little personality. But the winery API isn't the real experiment. The production workflow is. I wanted something small enough to understand end to end, yet realistic enough to expose the places where documents drift apart.

The rules were already knowable

The hard part isn't generating text. It's keeping the outputs consistent with the source.

A language model could read a script and draft separate production documents. That introduces an interpretive step, and for this workflow there is nothing to interpret. A [SCREENCAST] section belongs in the screencast document. An [ONSET] section belongs in the presenter document. An [ACTION] is a production instruction and a [VOICEOVER] is spoken narration. The generator does not need to decide what the author meant each time it runs, because the author already said so in the markup.

So the project uses a small, explicit grammar. The master script organizes content by stage and video, with tagged production sections and annotations inside them. Those tags are instructions to a parser, not prompts asking a model to infer structure.

Figure 1. The master script organizes content by stage and video, with tagged production sections inside each.

Worth being clear about what this is and isn't an argument for. I used an AI coding agent heavily while building this thing. What I didn't do was leave one in the pipeline. Those are different decisions, and conflating them is how you end up with an interpretive layer in a transformation whose rules you could have written down. Use a model where the rules aren't knowable. Where they are, write the rules.

A parser turns the source into a structured intermediate representation. Validation checks that sections are well formed and that the expected course structure is present. Only then does the generator prepare outputs.

Figure 2. The pipeline. Validation sits between parsing and any Drive write, so a malformed source produces diagnostics instead of documents.

The separation matters. Parsing establishes what the document says structurally. Validation decides whether it is safe to proceed. Estimation calculates values under stated assumptions. Rendering turns validated data into documents for different readers. None of those steps needs to invent missing content.

One source, different readers

The example course contains two stages, six videos, and thirteen production sections: six ONSET, three MOTION, four SCREENCAST. Some videos combine a presenter introduction with a screencast. Others use motion graphics, or return to the presenter after a demonstration.

That last case is the useful one for testing. "Handling Errors," the second video of stage two, runs ONSET → MOTION → SCREENCAST → ONSET, which means a single video contains two distinct presenter segments separated by other production material. The generated ONSET document identifies them as Part 1 of 2 and Part 2 of 2 rather than running them together as though the presenter never left.

The ONSET document carries narration and pause cues without the screencast directions. The SCREENCAST document preserves the sequence of actions, highlights, and voiceover, including example API requests and JSON responses. The MOTION document serves the animation role. The Production Summary provides counts, estimates, and warnings across the course.

Figure 3. Each run creates a new folder: four role-specific documents plus the manifest that records how they were made.

Figure 4. The same source, two readers. The presenter gets narration and pause cues. The screencast producer gets actions, examples, and voiceover.

These aren't four independently authored interpretations of the script. They are four views of the same validated structure. An editor changes the master document and runs generation again, and the previous output set remains a snapshot of the earlier run.

A validation gate before any Drive writes

The most important feature may be what happens when the source is wrong.

The project includes deliberately malformed script fixtures: missing closing tags, unexpected closing tags, nested production sections, unknown annotations. The parser returns diagnostics with source locations rather than trying to repair the document silently. Validation runs before output creation, so a malformed source blocks generation and the workflow never produces a polished-looking set of documents from a broken script.

That's a modest rule. It's also the difference between automation that produces files and automation that enforces a contract.

It also creates a useful exercise: introduce an error into a copy of the master script, read the diagnostic, confirm that generation is blocked, correct the source, run validation again. The failure is part of the lesson rather than something to hide from the learner.

A polished success path shows what a tool can do. A controlled failure shows what the system actually guarantees, where the boundary sits, and how to recover. I've written before about tests that cannot fail, and a generation step with no negative control has the same problem: it certifies nothing, confidently.

Estimation is not observation

The fourth document adds a production estimate. The estimator counts spoken words from ONSET narration and VOICEOVER blocks, excluding directions such as ACTION, VISUAL, and HIGHLIGHT. At the default assumption of 140 words per minute, it calculates narration duration per video, and videos over a configurable threshold get a warning.

That sounds straightforward until the numbers acquire an undeserved aura of precision. A word count is an observed property of the script under a counting rule. A duration is a calculation from an assumed speaking rate. Actual recording time includes pauses, interactions, retakes, animation, and editing choices the model doesn't capture.

So the Production Summary states its rules rather than describing them. The counting rule, verbatim from the generated document:

A word is a whitespace-separated token with at least one letter or digit. Contractions, hyphenated terms, numbers, and URLs or code in narration each count as one word, as written.

It also states its rounding policy: durations round to the nearest second for display, while totals and the threshold check use unrounded values, so a displayed value can sit exactly at the threshold and the displayed per-video figures may not add up precisely to the total.

And where an assumption has no evidence behind it, it says so. The screencast allowance is configurable and currently set to zero seconds per section, which makes every figure a narration-only estimate. The document is explicit that this "isn't a claim that screen actions take no time; no evidence-based figure has been set." I find that distinction worth more than a plausible guess would be.

Figure 5. The Production Summary: counted words, estimated duration, and threshold status per video, with the assumptions stated underneath.

In the current live run, the six videos contain 1,978 counted spoken words and an estimated 14 minutes 8 seconds of narration at 140 words per minute. One video trips the three-minute warning: "Handling Errors," at 664 words and 4 minutes 45 seconds. The hardest video to parse correctly turns out to be the one the estimator flags as too long, which is a coincidence I enjoyed more than I should have.

An earlier run counted 1,980 words. An editorial revision reduced the count by two, which is exactly the kind of drift the manifest exists to make legible.

The estimator also annotates counts that deserve suspicion. Four of the six videos carry notes like "includes 2 URL, path, or code tokens that may take longer to narrate," because a URL read aloud is one word by the counting rule and considerably more than one word of speech.

The point isn't that 14 minutes 8 seconds will be the final course runtime. It's that the estimate is reproducible, its assumptions are visible, and a change to it can be explained.

The manifest is part of the deliverable

Every generation run creates a new output folder rather than overwriting an earlier set. Alongside the four Google Docs, a JSON manifest records the source document reference and the hash of its text, the parser and estimator versions and their hashes, the configuration, output references, counts, and warnings.

{
  "schemaVersion": 2,
  "status": "complete",
  "runId": "e628c57a",
  "generatedAt": "2026-11-17T17:05:57.809Z",
  "source": {
    "documentId": "1WSw...zh4",
    "documentUrl": "https://docs.google.com/open?id=1WSw...zh4",
    "documentTitle": "Digital Cellar - Master Production Script",
    "lastUpdated": "2026-11-17T17:03:46.454Z",
    "extractedTextSha256": "bd8dfd4e8366f0b42b1ecaf381a9b5d44cee7412673aedeaf01108e366fa2c8a",
    "extractedLineCount": 410
  },
  "parser": {
    "version": "0.1.0",
    "coreSha256": "b5c678e69a36b1fd655d61b454eea156b37b78d839ec1342d34c27dab61ec8fc"
  },
  "estimator": {
    "schemaVersion": 1,
    "version": "0.1.0",
    "coreSha256": "00343c8a147b1792db7b840a80b91ce25fe194aa8a7ab0d382b38506770e08bd",
    "config": {
      "wordsPerMinute": 140,
      "longVideoThresholdMinutes": 3,
      "screencastAllowanceSecondsPerSection": 0
    }
  },
  "output": {
    "folderId": "1hRU...EEE",
    "folderUrl": "https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1hRU...EEE",
    "folderName": "Digital Cellar Production — 2026-11-17 170557 UTC — e628c57a",
    "documents": [
      // four entries, one per generated document
    ]
  }
  // counts and warnings follow
}

Figure 6. The run manifest. Document identifiers are truncated; the hashes and configuration are as generated.

That manifest doesn't prove the narration is pedagogically effective, or that a human approved every sentence. It establishes something narrower and more useful: which source and which transformation logic produced a particular set of artifacts. If two runs differ, there's a record to investigate instead of file modification times and memory.

The distinction matters because it's easy to oversell. A record of what a system did is not a judgment that what it did was right. It just means the question has an answer.

The generated documents carry a notice that edits made there do not flow back into the master. That boundary prevents a common misunderstanding: a derived document is not a second authoritative copy simply because Google Docs makes it editable.

Where the implementation stays small

The parser and estimator are portable JavaScript components tested outside Google Apps Script. The Google integration handles document extraction, formatting, Drive operations, and manifest creation. Automated tests cover parsing, estimation, and the Apps Script adapter with service doubles, though live Google Docs runs are still necessary to verify actual formatting and authorization behavior.

The master Google Doc can also use native heading and title styles without changing the transformation, because the parser works from the extracted text and explicit annotations rather than the document's visual formatting.

The limits are real and chosen. The source grammar has no explicit code-example annotation yet, so the screencast renderer uses a documented convention for examples following certain direction lines, which works for this course and is not a universal code detector. The runtime estimate is not a scheduling model. The project doesn't synchronize edits back from generated documents, and it doesn't use a model to interpret the script during generation.

A teaching project gets harder to understand when every possible extension is implemented before anyone can reproduce the core workflow.

The lab, and why the teaching material is tested too

The published learning lab offers a roughly one-hour, local-first path from inspection to verification, plus an optional Google Docs generation extension. Learners don't need a Google account for the core exercises.

The sequence moves from inspection to verification. Examine the structured script. Parse it locally. Compare its structure against an independently maintained fixture. Deliberately break a tag and read the diagnostic. Change an estimation assumption and see what moves. Compare two example manifests. Then, optionally, connect a Google account and generate a real run.

The part I'm most pleased with is less visible: the lab's instructional commands and expected outputs are checked against the repository in CI. If the implementation changes and the teaching material stops matching it, the build fails. Documentation drifting away from the code it documents is the same failure as four production documents drifting away from one script, and it would have been faintly embarrassing to write this article without closing that loop. The teaching material is held to the contract it teaches.

The automation could have stopped at four Google Docs and a manifest. But a working project becomes more useful when someone else can reproduce its behavior, including the failures. That's the progression I tend to favor: inspect the system, change one thing, observe the result, explain the evidence. It asks a better question than "did the script run?" The better question is can you explain exactly why this output differs from the previous one?

Open the learning lab

Explore the source repository

Where else would this approach help?

A production script is one instance of a broader pattern: one structured source, several audiences, and a set of transformations that should not quietly disagree. The interesting question isn't whether we can generate more files. It's whether the outputs share enough rules that the transformations can be described explicitly and tested.

A developer workshop is the closest neighbor. The instructor needs a facilitator guide with timing and teaching notes. Participants need exercises without the answers. A teaching assistant needs checkpoints and troubleshooting guidance. One underlying body of workshop content could produce all three, with deliberate rules about what belongs where, and a changed command wouldn't require three people to remember three documents.

Certification and assessment programs are the more interesting case, because they add a constraint this project never had to face. A structured question bank could support candidate assessments, reviewer keys, topic coverage reports, and versioned release packages. But now the transformation rules carry a security requirement: answers must never reach candidate materials. That's an argument for stronger, more explicitly tested boundaries, not against the pattern. A rule you can state is a rule you can test, and "the candidate document contains no ANSWER blocks" is a very testable rule.

Documentation sets, release records, and onboarding programs have similar shapes, with different readers drawing on facts that ought to stay consistent.

None of this means every paragraph should live in one enormous master file. Some material genuinely needs separate authorship and editorial judgment. The approach earns its keep where the shared facts, the roles, and the transformation rules are explicit enough to validate. Where the rules aren't knowable, deterministic generation is the wrong tool, or at most one part of the workflow.

What this experiment demonstrated

A single source of truth is not just a file everyone agrees to edit. It needs a defined structure, validation rules, reproducible transformations, and clear boundaries around derived artifacts. Otherwise "one source" is a convention people can violate by accident.

This project started with a fictional winery API and a six-video course script. It ended with a small document production pipeline: one structured input, four role-specific Google Docs, a validation gate, deterministic runtime estimates, and a manifest for each run.
