Whenever several teams need different views of the same underlying content, the first question may not be how to write each document faster. It may be how to stop writing the same facts four times.

The winery theme made the example more enjoyable. The reproducible workflow is the part I'd reuse.

The code and the lab are both on GitHub. If you try either, a star is a useful signal: whether this gets a second version depends on whether the pattern is useful to anyone besides me, and I’d rather settle that with evidence than a hunch.

Open the learning lab · Star the repository

If you’ve solved a version of this coordination problem differently, I’d like to hear it. That’s the thread I’d most want in the comments.

articles.title: Video autoplay blocked? Handle the play() promise, fall back to muted, and test it honestly
articles.description: TL;DR   video.play() is a request, and the browser can say no. We'll reproduce the...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

video.play() is a request, and the browser can say no. We'll reproduce the rejection, build a three-step fallback (sound, muted, play button), and write a Playwright test that sees what a first-time visitor sees. Tested on Playwright 1.63.0 with Chromium 153.

📦 Code: github.com/USER/repo (replace before publishing)

What we're building 🎥

A hero video that tries to play with sound, settles for muted playback with a "Tap to unmute" button when the browser refuses, and shows a plain play button if even that fails. Then a test that proves it, without the test harness quietly handing us a user gesture.

You need Node 22, Playwright, and FFmpeg to make a test clip:

npm i -D playwright
ffmpeg -f lavfi -i testsrc2=size=1280x720:rate=30:duration=10 \
       -f lavfi -i sine=frequency=440:duration=10 \
       -c:v libvpx-vp9 -b:v 1M -c:a libopus clip.webm

💡 Tip: Playwright's bundled Chromium has no H.264 or AAC decoder. Use VP9 and Opus in WebM for test fixtures or your test will fail for the wrong reason.

Serve the folder with any static server on port 8080 (npx serve -l 8080 works).

1. Reproduce the rejection

Start with the naive page. Playback is started by the page itself, with no interaction:

<!-- selfplay.html -->
<!doctype html>
<video id="v" src="clip.webm" playsinline></video>
<script>
  const v = document.getElementById('v');
  v.muted = new URLSearchParams(location.search).has('muted');
  window.result = null;
  v.play()
    .then(() => { window.result = { ok: true, muted: v.muted }; })
    .catch((e) => { window.result = { ok: false, name: e.name, message: e.message }; });
</script>

Load it in headless Chromium and read window.result:

in-page play(), unmuted: {"ok":false,"name":"NotAllowedError","message":"play() failed because the user didn't interact with the document first. https://goo.gl/xX8pDD"}
in-page play(), muted:   {"ok":true,"muted":true}

That is the whole policy in two lines. Muted is allowed, audible is not, and the refusal arrives as a rejected promise named NotAllowedError.

2. Know the rules you are coding against

From the Chrome autoplay policy, the MDN autoplay guide, and WebKit's video policies for iOS:

Situation What happens
Muted video, or no audio track Allowed to autoplay in Chrome, Safari and Firefox
Audible video, no interaction yet play() rejects with NotAllowedError
Audible video after a click or tap on the page Allowed
Chrome desktop, site with a high Media Engagement Index Audible autoplay allowed
<video autoplay> attribute is blocked Nothing fires. No event, no error
iOS Safari, unmuting without a gesture Playback pauses
iPhone without playsinline Video wants fullscreen; MDN lists playsinline as required for autoplay in Safari
Cross-origin iframe Needs allow="autoplay" from the parent

Two of these explain most bug reports:

  • "Works on my machine." Chrome's Media Engagement Index counts plays longer than seven seconds with unmuted audio in an active tab, on a video larger than 200x140 px. You have done that on your own site many times. New visitors have not. Check yours at about://media-engagement.
  • The silent attribute. I left an unmuted <video autoplay> alone for one second and read its state: {"paused":true,"currentTime":0,"error":null}. There is nothing to catch. If your UI needs to know the outcome, call play() yourself.

3. Write the fallback 🛠️ 

// autoplay.js
export async function startPlayback(video) {
  try {
    await video.play();              // 1. ask for sound
    return 'playing';
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name !== 'NotAllowedError') throw err;
  }
  video.muted = true;
  try {
    await video.play();              // 2. settle for silence
    return 'playing-muted';
  } catch {
    return 'blocked';                // 3. wait for a real gesture
  }
}

Only NotAllowedError triggers the fallback. A NotSupportedError (bad source, missing codec) is a different problem and muting will not fix it, so we rethrow.

4. Wire the UI to events, not to intent 

<!-- hero.html -->
<!doctype html>
<video id="hero" src="clip.webm" playsinline loop></video>
<button id="unmute" hidden>🔊 Tap to unmute</button>
<button id="play" hidden>▶ Play</button>

<script type="module">
  import { startPlayback } from './autoplay.js';

  const video = document.getElementById('hero');
  const unmute = document.getElementById('unmute');
  const play = document.getElementById('play');

  // UI state follows what the element reports, never what we asked for.
  video.addEventListener('playing', () => { document.body.dataset.video = 'playing'; });
  video.addEventListener('pause', () => { document.body.dataset.video = 'paused'; });

  const outcome = await startPlayback(video);
  document.body.dataset.autoplay = outcome;
  unmute.hidden = outcome !== 'playing-muted';
  play.hidden = outcome !== 'blocked';

  // Unmute synchronously inside the click handler so the gesture still counts.
  unmute.addEventListener('click', () => { video.muted = false; unmute.hidden = true; });
  play.addEventListener('click', () => { video.muted = false; video.play(); play.hidden = true; });
</script>

Things to notice:

  • The play/pause icon in a real player should be driven by playing and pause events. Setting "playing" when you call play() is how you end up with a pause icon over a frozen frame.
  • video.muted = false runs directly in the handler. Don't await anything before it.
  • We write the outcome to data-autoplay on <body>. That gives CSS and tests something to read.

5. The test that lies

Here is the obvious Playwright test, and it is wrong:

// naive.mjs
const result = await page.evaluate(async () => {
  const v = document.querySelector('video');
  try { await v.play(); return 'played, muted=' + v.muted; }
  catch (e) { return e.name; }
});
console.log(result);

played, muted=false

Unmuted playback, no rejection, with the same default policy that rejected our inline script in step 1.

⚠️ Note: Code you run through page.evaluate() behaves as if a user gesture is active. Any play() you trigger from the test harness skips the autoplay policy. It can never show you what a cold visitor sees.

6. The test that tells the truth

Let the page start itself, and only observe:

// autoplay.test.mjs
import { chromium } from 'playwright';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

const cases = [
  { name: 'cold visitor (default policy)', args: [], expect: 'playing-muted' },
  { name: 'policy disabled', args: ['--autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required'], expect: 'playing' },
];

for (const c of cases) {
  const browser = await chromium.launch({ args: c.args });
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto('http://localhost:8080/hero.html');

  // Observe only. The page started playback by itself.
  await page.waitForSelector('body[data-autoplay]');
  const outcome = await page.getAttribute('body', 'data-autoplay');
  const state = await page.getAttribute('body', 'data-video');
  const unmuteVisible = await page.isVisible('#unmute');
  console.log(`${c.name}: autoplay=${outcome} video=${state} unmuteButton=${unmuteVisible}`);
  assert.equal(outcome, c.expect);

  if (outcome === 'playing-muted') {
    await page.click('#unmute');                       // a real, trusted click
    const after = await page.evaluate(() => {
      const v = document.getElementById('hero');
      return { muted: v.muted, paused: v.paused };
    });
    console.log('  after click:', JSON.stringify(after));
    assert.deepEqual(after, { muted: false, paused: false });
  }
  await browser.close();
}
console.log('ok');

$ node autoplay.test.mjs
cold visitor (default policy): autoplay=playing-muted video=playing unmuteButton=true
  after click: {"muted":false,"paused":false}
policy disabled: autoplay=playing video=playing unmuteButton=false
ok

Reading state through page.evaluate() is fine. Starting playback through it is not. page.click() is the right way to unmute, because it dispatches a trusted input event, the same as a person would.

The --autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required flag comes from Chrome's own docs and is handy for the "returning, engaged user" case.

Things to know before you ship

  • Don't unmute from a timer. On iOS, WebKit pauses a muted autoplaying video that becomes audible without a gesture.
  • Offscreen video. WebKit only plays autoplay-attribute videos while visible and pauses them when scrolled away. Don't fight it. Pair muted autoplay with an IntersectionObserver if you need consistent behavior elsewhere.
  • navigator.getAutoplayPolicy() returns allowed, allowed-muted or disallowed. MDN marks it experimental, and in my Chromium 153 run typeof navigator.getAutoplayPolicy was undefined. Feature-detect it and keep the promise fallback.
  • Web Audio is covered too. An AudioContext created before a gesture starts suspended. Call resume() from a click.
  • This run was Chromium only. I did not rerun Safari or Firefox for this post. The table above is from their documentation, so test on real devices before you rely on the iOS rows.

What's next

  • Add the cold-visitor test to CI and assert your page never ends in a state outside playing, playing-muted or blocked.
  • If your video lives in a cross-origin iframe (embeds, ad slots), read the Permissions-Policy: autoplay section of the MDN guide next. That is the next wall you will hit.

articles.title: Which JavaScript table library? We built the same table nine times so you don't have to
articles.description: We needed a new JS table library for DataHub's dataset preview: has to show a CSV of anywhere from a...
articles.body_html:
We needed a new JS table library for DataHub's dataset preview: has to show a CSV of anywhere from a hundred rows to half a million.

I went looking for a comparison of table libraries and found lists: a dozen names, a feature matrix, no demos, and often a closing paragraph that just said: "it depends".

So we built a proper comparison:

https://tables.datahub.io

What to use

Here's what we'd use.

Job Use Runner-up
A table on a page (up to a few thousand rows) Plain <table> Observable Inputs
A big grid (up to 500,000 rows, sort and filter built in) AG Grid Community RevoGrid
An editable grid (edit cells, paste ranges) Tabulator RevoGrid

If you are in React and want your own markup and CSS, use TanStack Table with a virtualizer. That is what DataHub does.

What we did

Eight libraries and a plain <table>, on the same UK Land Registry sales data at 1,000 rows, 1,000 rows by 80 columns, 50,000 and 500,000, with the same harness and cell formatter. We measured gzipped bundle size, lines written, render time, scroll FPS, sort at 500,000 rows, text selection, keyboard sort and a small edit test. We also checked 13 features per library: see the compare page.

What we found

Speed doesn't pick a winner. Five grids (Glide, RevoGrid, TanStack, Tabulator, AG Grid) render 500,000 rows in 17 to 233 ms, scroll at 60 fps and sort by price in 0.1 to 0.42 s. Glide has no built-in sort, so its 0.1 s is our own code. Perspective takes 1.9 s and DataTables 8.5 s (its own FAQ says stop at about 50,000 rows).

Four other things separated them.

Text you can find and copy. Every grid except Glide, which is canvas, puts visible cells in the DOM, so Ctrl-F finds them. Only those: a virtualized grid has the rest unmounted. Browser text selection works in the plain table, Observable, Tabulator, TanStack and DataTables. AG Grid blocks it unless you set enableCellTextSelection; Perspective and RevoGrid block it. For a data site this is most of the job.

Weight. From 1 kB for a plain <table> to 332 kB for AG Grid. The chart has the rest.

How it fails. Tabulator's height: "100%", the pattern its docs give for filling a container, renders every row when the parent has no resolved height: 88 seconds at 50,000 rows against 36 ms with a sized parent, and nothing logged. AG Grid, given the same mistake, draws a visibly empty grid.

Whether it's still shipping. Glide Data Grid's last stable release was February 2024 and it is React 16 to 18 only. Our first draft picked it for large data. We reversed that.

The picks

A table on a page: plain <table>. 39 lines, 1 kB, 1,000 rows in about 55 ms. It prints, it copies, dark mode is CSS. But it lays out every row: 2.5 s at 50,000. For sort on click in one call, use Inputs.table(rows) from Observable and keep it under about ten thousand rows.

A big grid: AG Grid Community. 40 lines for sort, filter and virtualization. It is 332 kB as the quick start ships it (272 kB lean). Community is MIT; grouping, pivot, range selection, clipboard and Excel export are Enterprise. Runner-up RevoGrid is the fastest DOM grid we measured at 500,000 rows (62 ms), with clipboard free, if you accept the "RevoGrid" link in the corner.

An editable grid: Tabulator. The test: double-click a price and type, then paste three lines onto a cell. Tabulator passed with options from its own spreadsheet example, all free and MIT. RevoGrid passed with no config. AG Grid Community edits a cell, but paste is Enterprise.

Build your own: TanStack Table with a virtualizer. Headless: it computes rows, sorting and columns and you write every element. Our demo is 150 lines. v9 is a redesign and its docs lag it.

What DataHub will use

TanStack Table with react-virtual, wrapped once as a <DataTable> component in PortalJS. We already ship React, so the table costs 24 kB, not 332, and the preview is text people can Ctrl-F and copy a postcode out of. In exchange we write dataset-wide search, keyboard handling and virtualization ourselves.

Method and caveats

Every figure is the median of five page loads on one M4 laptop in headless Chromium, so treat them as an order of magnitude and re-measure in your own browser. The Tabulator 88 seconds was timed by hand. Agents built and measured the demos under our direction; we chose the verdict. Here are the script and the raw runs.

Try it

All nine are live, with source and the measure buttons:

https://tables.datahub.io

Tell us what we got wrong or missed.

Same treatment for line charts: linecharts.datahub.io.

Contains HM Land Registry data, Crown copyright and database right 2026, Open Government Licence v3.0.

Originally published on the DataHub blog.

articles.title: A game map in MapLibre, and share links in 7 characters
articles.description: I'm building a fan map of Leonida, the state in GTA 6. About 3,700 places, drawn with MapLibre GL....
articles.body_html:
I'm building a fan map of Leonida, the state in GTA 6. About 3,700 places, drawn with MapLibre GL. MapLibre wants real longitude and latitude. A game world has neither, so here's how I bent it into shape.

Fake the globe

The game data is in metres, from -16,384 to 16,384 on both axes. Web Mercator is a square too. So I stretch the game square over the whole Mercator square and treat lng/lat as a carrier, not a place on Earth:

const WORLD = 16384;

export function toLngLat(x, y) {
  const u = (x + WORLD) / (2 * WORLD);
  const v = (WORLD - y) / (2 * WORLD);
  return [u * 360 - 180, Math.atan(Math.sinh(Math.PI * (1 - 2 * v))) * 180 / Math.PI];
}

Everything is stored in game metres. Only this one file knows about lat/lng.

A nice side effect: the community tiles from GTADB (CC BY 4.0) line up with standard XYZ tiles, just shifted by two zoom levels. At the deepest level one pixel is half a metre.

The catch is that MapLibre's idea of distance is now meaningless. No scale bar. I measure in game metres myself.

Share links

People send each other "the safe is here" links all the time. #@25.7612,-80.1918,5.5 works, but it looks awful in a chat.

Round the centre to 4 m and each axis has 8,192 steps, so 13 bits. Zoom to one decimal fits in 7 bits. That's 33 bits, and 36^7 is about 78 billion, so a whole view fits in 7 base-36 characters:

function viewCode(lat, lng, zoom) {
  const [x, y] = fromLngLat(lng, lat);
  const q = (v) => Math.max(0, Math.min(8191, Math.round((v + WORLD) / 4)));
  const z = Math.max(0, Math.min(127, Math.round((zoom + 2) * 10)));
  return ((q(x) * 8192 + q(y)) * 128 + z).toString(36).padStart(7, '0');
}

A single place is a 5-character hash of its ID. Old long links still parse.

Don't make phones wait for the map

This one mattered most. On a phone, a first-time visitor sat on a loading screen for 6 to 10 seconds while the map library, every place and the icon sprite came in.

Now the HTML ships a small picture of the island, with the popular guide spots as plain links on top. They're positioned with the same maths the map uses, so when MapLibre fades in over them nothing moves. Tap a spot before the map is ready and it's just a link.

The heavy files are marked in the page and only start loading once the first screen is drawn:

for (const l of document.querySelectorAll('link[data-later]')) {
  const n = document.createElement('link');
  n.rel = l.dataset.later;
  n.as = l.getAttribute('as');
  n.href = l.getAttribute('href');
  document.head.append(n);
}

In the same test, the popular spots now show at 1.5 s instead of 5.1 s. The full map arrives 0.4 s later than before. I'll take that.

The map is at gta-6-map.org if you want to poke at it.

articles.title: Audio tools that never upload: Whisper, LAME and FLAC in the browser
articles.description: I built Scissor Audio, a set of free audio tools that run entirely in the browser:...
articles.body_html:
I built Scissor Audio, a set of free audio tools that run entirely in the browser: https://audio.scissor.studio/
You can trim, join, mix, convert, compress, transcribe and tag audio, and the file never leaves your device.

There are twelve tools and an audio editor, in 30 languages. Here is how the parts fit together, and where they stop.

A static site and plain modules

There is no framework and no backend for the audio. One Node script builds every page from a list of tools and a JSON file per language: the HTML, the head tags, the structured data and the service worker. Each tool is an ES module that the page loads when you open it. The site is served as static files from Cloudflare.

The server sends files and receives anonymous page counts and error reports. Opening, editing and saving all happen in the tab.

Decoding is the browser's job

I do not ship my own decoders. The browser already has them, and some formats are covered by patents I do not want to deal with. Every file goes through the Web Audio API and comes out as 44.1 kHz float samples:

export async function decode(file) {
  const ctx = new OfflineAudioContext(2, 1, 44100);
  const buf = await ctx.decodeAudioData(await file.arrayBuffer());
  return { rate: buf.sampleRate, ch: Array.from({ length: Math.min(2, buf.numberOfChannels) }, (_, i) => buf.getChannelData(i)) };
}

Decoding everything to the same rate means the joiner and the mixer can line tracks up sample for sample without resampling them again. The cost is memory: an hour of stereo audio is about 1.3 GB once decoded, so very long files can be too much for a phone.

Encoders: some borrowed, one written by hand

For MP3 the site uses LAME, and for Ogg it uses libvorbis, both compiled to WebAssembly by the wasm-media-encoders project. LAME is LGPL 2.1, so mp3.wasm (133 KB) stays a separate file that anyone can replace with their own build, and the licence page says where it came from. libvorbis and libogg are BSD 3-Clause; ogg.wasm is 450 KB. Both load only when you save in that format.

M4A uses the browser's own AAC encoder through WebCodecs, with a small MP4 writer around it. WAV is a header and the samples.

FLAC I wrote myself, because a lossless encoder is small when you keep it simple: 16-bit samples, fixed predictors and Rice coding, with the CRC-8 and CRC-16 each frame needs. It does not reach the compression of the reference encoder, but it is lossless and it is about 100 lines.

Speech models on the device

Audio to text runs OpenAI's Whisper base model (MIT) through transformers.js (Apache-2.0) and ONNX Runtime Web (MIT), quantized to 8 bits, in a web worker on WebAssembly, with threads where the browser allows them. The download is about 80 MB: a 23 MB encoder, a 54 MB decoder and a 2.5 MB tokenizer, all served from the same site.

Text to speech uses Kokoro 82M (Apache-2.0), about 92 MB. The bundle that turns text into phonemes contains eSpeak NG, which is GPL 3.0, so that one file is distributed under the GPL with its sources named.

Each model downloads once and stays in the browser's storage, so it then works offline. In Chrome, Edge and Firefox the Scissor tools share one copy, so the second tool that needs Whisper does not download it again.

The one request that leaves the page

The tag editor reads and writes ID3, MP4 and FLAC tags itself, and saves the same audio bytes with new tags. It can also look tags up in MusicBrainz. Apart from Google Drive, if you choose to open or save there, that is the only time the page talks to another server, and only when you press Search. What it sends is the words in the two search boxes. The cover comes from the Cover Art Archive.

The Content-Security-Policy lists exactly those hosts in connect-src, so nothing else can be fetched even by mistake.

Limits

  • Whisper base is small. It is fine for clear speech and weaker on noise, accents and names than the larger models. On an older phone a long recording takes a while, since it runs on the CPU.
  • The first transcription needs that 80 MB download.
  • Safari and browsers on iPhone keep a separate copy of the models for each site.
  • Which formats open depends on the browser, because decoding is the browser's.
  • M4A output needs the browser's AAC encoder; where it is missing, M4A is not offered.
  • The tag editor does not handle WAV or OGG tags yet.

Try it: https://audio.scissor.studio/

It is free, with no account and no sign-up. One question I would like answered: if you try audio to text on a phone, how long does one minute of speech take on your device, and which phone is it?

articles.title: Zip, 7z and RAR in the browser with libarchive compiled to WebAssembly
articles.description: I made Scissor Zip, a set of archive tools that run in the browser tab: https://zip.scissor.studio....
articles.body_html:
I made Scissor Zip, a set of archive tools that run in the browser tab: https://zip.scissor.studio. It zips files, adds AES-256 passwords, opens RAR, 7z and tar.gz, and converts between formats, with libarchive compiled to WebAssembly doing the work on your device.

The engine

The engine is libarchive 3.8.10, the library behind bsdtar, built with Emscripten together with the compression libraries it needs:

  • zlib 1.3.2 (zlib licence)
  • bzip2 1.0.8 (BSD-style)
  • XZ Utils 5.8.4, liblzma only (0BSD)
  • Zstandard 1.5.7 (BSD-3-Clause)
  • LZ4 1.10.0 (BSD-2-Clause)
  • Mbed TLS 3.6.5 (Apache-2.0), for the AES-256 encryption of password-protected zips

A small C file in front of libarchive exposes about twenty functions: open a buffer, step through entries, read one, write a new archive. The result is archive.wasm at 1.16 MB, about 324 KB with Brotli, plus a 67 KB JavaScript loader. It runs in a module worker, so a 500 MB archive does not freeze the page.

All of that is permissive licensing, and the licences page lists each component with its full text in a notices file next to the engine.

RAR, and what that means for licences

RAR is the part people ask about. libarchive reads RAR and RAR5 with its own code: archive_read_support_format_rar.c (Andres Mejia) and archive_read_support_format_rar5.c (Grzegorz Antoniak), both under the BSD 2-Clause licence. No RARLAB UnRAR source is involved, so there is no UnRAR licence to carry.

That also sets the limits. libarchive can read RAR but not write it, and RAR is a closed format that only WinRAR may create. So Scissor Zip extracts RAR and converts it to zip, 7z or tar, but never makes a .rar. Encrypted RAR and 7z archives do not open yet; the page says so instead of failing quietly.

Multi-part RAR archives (name.part1.rar, name.part2.rar, ...) work when you choose all the parts together. Each part has its own headers, so they cannot simply be joined. The C side gives libarchive one buffer per volume with archive_read_append_callback_data, plus read, seek and switch callbacks, and libarchive moves from part to part itself. Split 7z and zip archives (.001, .002, ...) are just bytes cut into pieces, so those parts are joined into one File in JavaScript before the engine sees them.

Telling a cut-short file from a broken engine

Big archives on phones are often incomplete: an interrupted download, or only the first part of a split set. libarchive reports that as "Seek error" or "Malformed 7-Zip archive", which used to reach the visitor as "the engine stopped". A 7z file says in its first 32 bytes how long it should be, so the worker checks that before reading the rest:

const head = new DataView((await readBytes(file, 0, 32)).buffer);
const want = 32 + Number(head.getBigUint64(12, true)) + Number(head.getBigUint64(20, true));
if (want > file.size) throw new Error(`PARTIAL: ${file.size}/${want}`);

The page then says the archive is incomplete, with both sizes, instead of blaming itself.

How the files stay on the device

The browser reads the chosen file with file.arrayBuffer(), copies it into the WebAssembly heap, and the result goes back as a Blob download. Our servers have no endpoint for your archives. The Content Security Policy only lets the page connect to its own origin, plus Google's sign-in and Drive services for the optional Google Drive open and save. The Drive scope is drive.file, so the site sees only files you open or save with it, and the Network tab in developer tools shows the rest.

Error reports carry a code such as ENGINE or MEMORY. When the code alone does not explain the error, the wording goes along too, but anything that looks like a file name or path is removed first.

A service worker keeps the pages and the engine, so a tool you have opened once works without a connection.

The limit: memory

Everything happens in the tab's memory. The archive is read into the WebAssembly heap, which can grow to 4 GB, and creating or converting holds the input and the new archive at the same time. Every out-of-memory report so far came from archives over 1 GB on desktop browsers, so the page now warns from 1 GB and suggests splitting. Streaming files through the engine in chunks would raise that ceiling, and it is the next big change I would like to make.

Try it

Try it: https://zip.scissor.studio

It is free, with no account and no ads, in 30 languages. There is also an archive explorer at /app/ that opens several archives side by side, previews images and text, and lets you add, rename or delete files before saving as zip, 7z or tar.

If you have an archive it fails to open, I would like to know the format and the tool that made it.

articles.title: I built a smart file assistant that never uploads your files. Here's how it works
articles.description: Most "free" file sites work the same way: you upload your photo or PDF, their server does the work,...
articles.body_html:
Most "free" file sites work the same way: you upload your photo or PDF, their server does the work, and you download the result. It works, but it's slow on a bad connection, there's usually a daily limit, and you're handing private files (ID scans, contracts, family photos) to a server you know nothing about.

When I started building DockFlip, I wanted to see how far I could get without a server ever touching the file. Turns out: pretty far. Here's how the main pieces work.

1. Compressing an image to an exact size (like "under 100 KB")

Forms love limits like "max 100 KB". Most compressors give you a quality slider and you guess.

The browser can already do the hard part:

  • Decode the file with createImageBitmap()
  • Draw it to a <canvas>
  • Re-encode it with canvas.toBlob(callback, 'image/jpeg', quality)

To hit a target size, I search for the quality instead of guessing: try the middle, check the blob size, move up or down, repeat a few times. If even a low quality can't get under the limit, scale the dimensions down a little and search again.

Here's a simplified version of the idea:

async function compressToTarget(bitmap, targetBytes) {
  const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
  canvas.width = bitmap.width;
  canvas.height = bitmap.height;
  canvas.getContext('2d').drawImage(bitmap, 0, 0);

  let lo = 0.05, hi = 0.95, best = null;
  for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
    const q = (lo + hi) / 2;
    const blob = await new Promise(r => canvas.toBlob(r, 'image/jpeg', q));
    if (blob.size <= targetBytes) { best = blob; lo = q; }
    else { hi = q; }
  }
  return best; // null means: resize and try again
}

Eight rounds is usually enough to land just under the limit with the best quality that still fits.

2. HEIC, PDFs and "Download all"

  • HEIC (iPhone photos): most browsers can't decode it natively, so a HEIC decoder is loaded only when someone opens a HEIC tool.
  • PDFs: pdf.js renders pages (PDF to JPG/PNG), and pdf-lib builds and merges PDFs (images to PDF, merge, split).
  • Many files at once: results are zipped with JSZip right in the browser, so there's one "Download all" button.

Lazy-loading matters here. Someone compressing one JPG shouldn't have to download a PDF engine.

3. A smart file assistant instead of a menu of 20 tools

With 20+ tools, the hard part isn't the conversion, it's finding the right page. So there's an assistant in the corner of every page: drop a file, type "pdf to jpg" or "compress to 50 kb", and it opens the right tool with your file already loaded.

It's not an LLM. It's simple intent matching on what you type, which is instant and runs locally. The file is passed to the tool page through IndexedDB, so it still never leaves the device.

Here's the assistant doing it in about 30 seconds:

What I learned

  • canvas + toBlob gets you surprisingly far before you need WebAssembly.
  • Load heavy libraries per tool, and keep the first page load light.
  • "Your file is never uploaded" is something people understand instantly. Privacy isn't a policy page here, it's just how the thing is built.
  • The limits are real: very large PDFs depend on the device's memory, and older phones are slower.

If you want to try it: dockflip.com (free, no sign-up).

I'd love feedback from other devs, especially on the target-size search. Would you do it differently?

articles.title: IA no código: onde ela realmente acelera (e onde só parece)
articles.description: Passei os últimos meses usando assistentes de IA no dia a dia — Claude, Copilot, e até ferramentas de linha de comando. A promessa é clara: "escreva menos,
articles.body_html:
Passei os últimos meses usando assistentes de IA no dia a dia — Claude, Copilot, e até ferramentas de linha de comando. A promessa é clara: "escreva menos, entregue mais rápido". Mas quando você olha o relógio no fim da sprint, será que economizou tempo de verdade?

A resposta curta: depende brutalmente do que você está fazendo. E ninguém fala dos casos onde você perde tempo.

O que mudou de fato

Tem tarefas onde IA é imbatível. Boilerplate, conversões de formato, testes repetitivos — coisas que você faria no piloto automático. Exemplo real: precisei migrar um monte de rotas Laravel de array config para a nova sintaxe fluente do 11.

Sem IA, eu teria aberto o arquivo, copiado um padrão, feito find-replace em 40 linhas, testado, commitado. 20 minutos, fácil.

Com IA:

// prompt: "converter estas rotas de array para Route::view() do Laravel 11"

// antes (config/routing.php)
'pricing' => [
    'view' => 'pages.pricing',
    'lastmod' => '2024-03-15',
],

// depois (routes/web.php) — gerado em 15 segundos
Route::view('/pricing', 'pages.pricing')
    ->middleware(['cache.headers:public;max_age=3600'])
    ->name('pricing');

Economizei 18 minutos? Não. Economizei energia cognitiva. A tarefa sumiu da minha pilha mental antes de eu perder o flow da coisa grande que estava fazendo. Isso vale mais que os minutos.

Onde IA realmente entrega velocidade

1. Scaffolding e estrutura inicial

Quando você sabe o que quer mas não lembra como escrever, IA te dá o esqueleto certo:

// prompt: "hook React que debounça input e faz fetch, com cleanup"

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

function useDebounceSearch(query, delay = 500) {
  const [results, setResults] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!query.trim()) {
      setResults([]);
      return;
    }

    setLoading(true);
    const timer = setTimeout(async () => {
      try {
        const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`);
        const data = await res.json();
        setResults(data);
      } catch (err) {
        console.error(err);
        setResults([]);
      } finally {
        setLoading(false);
      }
    }, delay);

    return () => clearTimeout(timer);
  }, [query, delay]);

  return { results, loading };
}

Isso não é código perfeito — você ainda vai ajustar error handling, adicionar tipos, tratar edge cases. Mas o padrão está lá. Você não gastou 10 minutos lembrando sintaxe de useEffect com cleanup.

2. Documentação inline e refatoração de legado

Herdei um controller Laravel com 300 linhas, zero comentários, variáveis $d e $r. Pedi pra IA:

"adicionar docblocks, renomear variáveis pra nomes descritivos, extrair lógica de validação pra método privado"

Resultado: código legível em 2 minutos. Eu teria levado 40 minutos fazendo isso manual, e provavelmente teria desistido no meio.

3. Testes que você não ia escrever

Sejamos honestos: quantas vezes você pulou testes unitários porque "é só um helper simples"? IA remove a friction:

// prompt: "testes PHPUnit pra este método, incluindo edge cases"

class UrlHelperTest extends TestCase
{
    /** @test */
    public function it_removes_trailing_slash()
    {
        $this->assertEquals('/pricing', normalizeUrl('/pricing/'));
    }

    /** @test */
    public function it_handles_empty_string()
    {
        $this->assertEquals('/', normalizeUrl(''));
    }

    /** @test */
    public function it_preserves_query_strings()
    {
        $this->assertEquals('/search?q=test', normalizeUrl('/search/?q=test'));
    }
}

Você ainda precisa rodar, ajustar asserções, adicionar casos que a IA esqueceu. Mas a barreira de "escrever o primeiro teste" sumiu.

Onde você perde tempo (e ninguém admite)

1. Código plausível mas errado

IA é excelente em gerar código que parece certo. Sintaxe válida, padrões conhecidos, até comentários explicativos. O problema: pode estar sutilmente errado.

Exemplo real que me custou 30 minutos: pedi um middleware Laravel pra bloquear países por geoIP. A IA gerou um código lindo, com early returns, logs, tudo. Só que usou request()->ip() direto — e no ambiente atrás de Cloudflare, isso sempre retorna o IP do proxy, não do cliente real.

A solução era request()->header('CF-Connecting-IP'), mas eu só descobri depois de deployar, ver que não funcionava, debugar, ler docs da Cloudflare, e corrigir.

Tempo gasto: 5 min gerando + 30 min debugando = 35 min.

Tempo que levaria escrevendo do zero: 20 min, porque eu teria lido a doc antes.

2. Prompt iteration hell

Quando o prompt não é preciso, você entra num loop:

  • Primeira tentativa: código genérico demais
  • Segunda: agora usa biblioteca errada
  • Terceira: sintaxe antiga da biblioteca
  • Quarta: finalmente próximo, mas faltam validações

Cada iteração parece barata — 20 segundos — mas você já queimou 5 minutos e ainda não tem código rodando. Se a tarefa não é repetitiva, escrever direto pode ser mais rápido.

3. Over-engineering gerado

IA adora abstrações. Pede "uma função que valida email" e ela te dá uma classe com interface, factory, 3 métodos privados e suporte a i18n. Pra um form de contato.

Você gasta tempo deletando 70% do código gerado e simplificando pro que realmente precisa.

O custo invisível: você para de aprender o ecossistema

Esse é o tradeoff mais sorrateiro. Quando IA gera o código, você não lê a documentação oficial, não vê exemplos alternativos, não entende por que aquele padrão existe.

No começo parece eficiência. Três meses depois, você está travado numa decisão arquitetural porque nunca mergulhou fundo na biblioteca — só usou o que a IA cuspiu.

Aprendi isso da pior forma: usando IA pra gerar queries Eloquent complexas. Funcionava, eu commitava, seguia em frente. Até o dia que precisei otimizar N+1 queries e percebi que não entendia o que with(), load() e loadMissing() faziam de diferente. Tive que parar tudo e ler a doc que deveria ter lido 2 meses atrás.

Quando usar (meu framework mental atual)

Depois de errar bastante, cheguei nesta heurística:

  • Use IA pra: boilerplate, testes, conversões mecânicas, refatoração de nomes, tradução entre sintaxes (jQuery → React, Python → JS).
  • Escreva você pra: lógica de negócio core, integrações com APIs externas (IA não conhece suas credenciais/ambiente), código que mexe com dinheiro ou dados sensíveis.
  • Use IA como rubber duck pra: planejar arquitetura antes de codar, revisar seu próprio código, gerar perguntas que você deveria fazer na doc.

TL;DR

  • IA economiza tempo real em tarefas mecânicas (boilerplate, testes, refatoração de legado)
  • Maior ganho não é velocidade bruta, é não perder flow com tarefas chatas
  • Código gerado parece certo mas pode ter bugs sutis de ambiente/contexto — sempre revisar
  • Prompt ruim = loop de iteração que consome mais tempo que escrever manual
  • Risco silencioso: você para de aprender o ecossistema e fica dependente de abstrações que não entende
  • Regra prática: IA pra mecânica, você pra lógica core e decisões arquiteturais

articles.title: Mermaid diagrams look dated? Not anymore!
articles.description: prettymaids restyles Mermaid diagrams with modern themes, dark mode, donut pies and XMind-style mindmaps, and keeps Mermaid's own layout. Here's how it works and what went wrong along the way.
articles.body_html:
Mermaid is everywhere now: READMEs, design docs, wikis, and whatever diagram your AI assistant just generated for you. It's a great tool, but the default output looks like it's from 2012. Flat outlines, tiny text, cramped spacing. The built-in themes only change colours.

I wanted Mermaid diagrams I'd be happy to put in a slide deck, so I built prettymaids: modern themes plus an SVG post-processor, wrapped around stock Mermaid.

You can try it right now, with nothing to install: pravin.github.io/prettymaids

The approach: keep Mermaid, restyle the output

The obvious way to get nicer diagrams is to write a new renderer. I decided against that. Mermaid's parser and layout engine handle a huge range of diagram types, and anyone with existing diagrams (or an AI tool that emits Mermaid) can keep their source unchanged.

So prettymaids leaves Mermaid alone and restyles in three layers:

  1. Theme variables and CSS: fonts, colours, borders, spacing.
  2. Per-diagram config: padding, node and rank spacing, label wrapping.
  3. A post-processor on the rendered SVG: the things CSS can't do.

That third layer is where most of the look comes from:

  • Stacked soft drop shadows via an SVG filter
  • Rounded corners on class and ER boxes, which Mermaid draws as sketch-style paths that CSS can't round
  • Donut charts instead of pies, done by clipping each slice to a ring
  • XMind-style mindmaps, with smooth S-curve branches that get thinner with depth and take the colour of their main topic
  • An optional dot-grid canvas behind everything

Three things that went wrong

1. My "connector style" setting did nothing

I added a setting to switch edges between rounded, elbow, straight and curved. In the playground, all four looked identical.

It turns out Mermaid 12's default layout routes its own rounded orthogonal edges and ignores the flowchart.curve option entirely. Only the dagre layout honours it. So the setting now switches layout engine when you pick anything other than the default.

I only noticed because I diffed the rendered SVG instead of trusting my eyes. If a style option "works" but you've never compared the output, check it.

2. Fonts bite you twice

Mermaid measures label text when it renders, then sizes the boxes to fit. I rendered with a font that wasn't installed locally, then viewed the result on a machine that had it. The real font was wider, and labels got clipped ("Receive reques").

The fixes:

  • Let labels overflow their container instead of clipping
  • In the browser playground, wait for the font to load before the first render
  • Install the font in CI, so the gallery renders with the real metrics

If you generate Mermaid SVGs on one machine and view them on another, this will happen to you too.

3. Different shapes need different padding

I wanted pills (terminal nodes) and decision nodes to be sized differently from ordinary boxes. But CSS can't change the box size after Mermaid has measured the text.

So flowcharts render twice. The first pass finds which nodes are pills or decisions. The second pass adds a class to each of them, so my CSS applies while Mermaid is measuring. That keeps the edges attached to the right places.

Ways to use it

In the browser: the playground has a live editor, three themes, about 28 parameters you can tune, and SVG or PNG export. The comparison gallery shows stock Mermaid next to each theme for every diagram type.

As a CLI:

npx prettymaids-cli diagram.mmd -o diagram.png

As a library:

npm install prettymaids mermaid

import mermaid from 'mermaid';
import { render, config } from 'prettymaids';

// Full look, including SVG post-processing:
const svg = await render(source, { theme: 'maid', mermaid });

// Or just the colours and typography, as a plain Mermaid config:
mermaid.initialize(config('maid'));

There are three themes: maid (light), maid-dark, and maid-flat, a lower-contrast flat look.

Honest limits

  • Decision diamonds stay square. Mermaid builds them that way, and changing it means writing a custom shape.
  • The CLI needs Chrome, because Mermaid needs a real browser to measure text. Installing the package downloads a Chromium for you.
  • GitHub, Obsidian and Notion render Mermaid themselves, so prettymaids can't restyle diagrams inside them. Render with the CLI and commit the image.
  • Nine diagram types are styled so far: flowchart, sequence, class, state, ER, gantt, pie, mindmap and git graph. Journey, timeline, quadrant and XY charts are unstyled for now.
  • It's tested against Mermaid 12.3.

Try it, and tell me what's next

  • Playground: https://pravin.github.io/prettymaids/
  • Repo (MIT): https://github.com/pravin/prettymaids

If you try it on a diagram that comes out wrong, please open an issue and paste the Mermaid source. And if you have a view on which diagram type or look I should do next, I'd like to hear it in the comments.

articles.title: Image tools in a 216 KB Rust WebAssembly engine, with no upload step
articles.description: I built Scissor Image, a set of 28 image tools that run in the browser:...
articles.body_html:
I built Scissor Image, a set of 28 image tools that run in the browser: https://image.scissor.studio/. Convert, compress to a size in KB, resize, crop, split, redact, remove photo location, filters and a QR code generator, in 30 languages.

The images never go to my server. The browser decodes them, a small Rust engine does the work, and the result is saved back to your device.

The split: the browser decodes, Rust does the rest

I did not want to ship decoders the browser already has. So a tool starts with createImageBitmap(file), draws the bitmap on a canvas and reads the RGBA pixels. That covers JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF and GIF, in whatever the browser supports.

Everything after that happens in the engine: resize, crop, rotate and flip, the round crop for profile pictures, encoding, metadata and the ZIP for batches. It is about 1,000 lines of Rust in four files, compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen and run in a Web Worker, so the page stays responsive on a large photo.

The release .wasm is 216 KB after wasm-opt -Oz.

The libraries

The engine depends on the image crate 0.25, with only the jpeg, png and webp features turned on. Through it come zune-jpeg, png, image-webp and miniz_oxide, plus crc32fast for the ZIP writer. All of them are MIT or Apache-2.0, with some also under Zlib or BSD-3-Clause. The QR code tool uses qrcode-generator (MIT) on the JavaScript side.

The build writes every licence text into one notices file from cargo metadata, and fails if a crate ships without one.

One limit: the image crate's WebP encoder is lossless only. So "convert to WebP" gives you a lossless WebP, which is often larger than the JPG you started from. JPG output has a quality setting; WebP does not, yet.

Compress to an exact size in KB

Four of the tools are "compress image to 20 KB / 50 KB / 100 KB / 200 KB", because exam and job forms ask for exactly that. A fixed quality setting does not work for this: the size depends on the photo.

So the engine searches. If the photo has far more pixels than the target can hold, it first scales down to roughly 24 pixels per byte of budget. Then it does a binary search over JPEG quality 40 to 95 and keeps the highest quality that fits:

let (mut lo, mut hi) = (40u8, 95u8);
while lo <= hi {
    let q = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    self.jpeg(q, background, &mut out)?;
    if out.len() <= max_bytes {
        best = Some(out);
        lo = q + 1;
    } else {
        hi = q - 1;
    }
}

If even quality 40 is too big, it shrinks the image by 15% and searches again.

Removing location without re-compressing

"Remove photo location" should not cost image quality. Re-encoding a JPG to drop its EXIF block would. So this tool does not touch the pixels at all: it edits the file's container. It finds the EXIF, XMP and IPTC segments, removes them, or only the GPS fields if you choose that, and copies the compressed image data across byte for byte.

How the images stay on the device

The site is static files. There is no endpoint that accepts an image, so there is nothing that could receive one. On top of that, the Content Security Policy only lets the page contact its own origin, and Google's sign-in and Drive APIs, which load only when you press Open from Drive or Save to Drive. Drive uses the drive.file scope, so the site can see only files you open or create with it.

The same origin also hosts a small service of mine for page counts, error reports and feedback forms. None of them carry image data or file names. The tools also work offline once the site has been opened, because a service worker stores the app and the engine.

HEIC, and where it stops

iPhone photos are HEIC: HEVC frames inside a HEIF container. HEVC is covered by patents, and I do not want to ship a decoder for it. So HEIC uses the browser's own decoder only.

Safari decodes HEIC natively. In Chrome and Edge, the page reads the HEIF container itself, finds the coded tiles (iPhone photos are a grid of 512 by 512 tiles), and gives each one to WebCodecs' VideoDecoder. That uses the HEVC decoder of the operating system or the GPU, which the platform has licensed. The tiles are drawn onto a canvas, then rotation, mirroring and crop are applied from the file.

Firefox has no HEVC in WebCodecs, and most Linux setups do not either. There, HEIC files are turned away with a short message that explains how to get JPGs from an iPhone instead. Recent iPhones also save 10-bit HDR photos, which need hardware that can decode 10-bit HEVC.

Try it: https://image.scissor.studio/

It is free, with no account and no watermark.

One question for you: if you open HEIC photos in Chrome or Edge on Windows or Android, do they open, and do the colours match what you see on the iPhone?
